facts.label: Peak vertical ground force and loading rate from walking to running (people)
facts.display: 1.2 × body weight at 1.5 m/s, rising linearly to about 2.5 × at 6 m/s; loading rate 8–30 body weights per second

sources.title: Keller et al. (1996), Relationship between vertical ground reaction force and speed during walking, slow jogging, and running, Clin Biomech 11:253 (PubMed 11415629), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'GRF-time histories were recorded for 13 male and 10 female recreational athletes during walking and slow jogging at speeds between 1.5 and 3.0 m s(-1), and running at speeds between 3.5 and 6.0 m s(-1).' 'F(z) increased linearly during walking and running from 1.2 BW to approximately 2.5 BW at 6.0 m s(-1) ... F(z) was linearly correlated to G(z), the latter ranging from 8 to 30 BW s(-1)'. 1.2 BW is the value at 1.5 m/s, the slowest walk tested. Slow jogging gave '>50% higher F(z) and G(z)' than walking. Agrees with walking_running_peak_vertical_force (Nilsson & Thorstensson 1989: 1.0 to 1.5 BW walking); supports W8.WALK_LOAD = 1.2. Verifier: quotes match; G(z) is undefined in the abstract but, being far below instantaneous rates (42-113 BW/s), is almost certainly an average rate. Our inference only: at 8 BW/s, 1.2 BW is reached in about 0.15 s.
facts.who_when: Keller, Weisberger, Ray, Hasan, Shiavi & Spengler 1996

facts.label: Normal (comfortable) human walking speed, meta-analysis: range of group means by age and sex
facts.display: Group means from 0.94 m/s (women aged 80–99) to 1.43 m/s (men aged 40–49); 23,111 people. The top figure is the fastest group, not a typical speed

sources.title: Bohannon & Williams Andrews (2011), Normal walking speed: a descriptive meta-analysis, Physiotherapy 97:182 (PubMed 21820535), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'Forty-one articles contributed data to the analysis. Combined, they provided data from 23111 subjects. The gait speed was homogeneous within strata and ranged from a mean of 143.4 cm/second for men aged 40 to 49 years to a mean of 94.3 cm/second for women aged 80 to 99 years.' Walks were 3 to 30 m long at a normal pace. The per-decade table is paywalled and was not read. Verifier: value_si was 1.43, the highest stratum mean, which overstates a 'normal' speed; set to null so the page shows the range. For young adults see step_fukuchi2018_preferred_froude (1.24 m/s, overground).

facts.label: Walking cadence (steps per minute) at set treadmill speeds, adults 21–40
facts.display: 113.6 steps/min at 3.0 mph (1.34 m/s); 96.1 at 2.0 mph; 129.0 at 4.0 mph

sources.title: Tudor-Locke et al. (2019), Walking cadence (steps/min) and intensity in 21–40 year olds: CADENCE-adults, IJBNPA 16:8 (PMC6337834), full text via Europe PMC

facts.notes: Table 'Sample sizes, cadences, VO2, and METs for treadmill bouts': '3.0 | 74 | 113.6 ± 6.1 | 101–127'; 2.0 mph 96.1 ± 6.5 (n 76); 4.0 mph 129.0 ± 7.6 (n 62). 76 healthy adults (38 men, 38 women), 5-minute treadmill bouts, cadence counted by hand. Leg length was standing minus seated height ('Leg length was then calculated by subtracting the seated height from standing height'), about 0.47 of stature; not hip-joint height. Treadmill, not overground. Verifier: bouts ended when people chose to run, or at more than 75% of predicted maximum heart rate, or at an RPE above 13, so the falling n at higher speeds is not purely walk-to-run selection.

facts.label: Comfortable walking speed as a Froude number (young adults, measured)
facts.display: Comfortable overground walking: Froude number 0.18 ± 0.04 (0.10–0.29), 1.24 m/s, leg 0.51 of height (24 young adults)

sources.title: Fukuchi, Fukuchi & Duarte (2018), A public dataset of overground and treadmill walking kinematics and kinetics in healthy individuals, PeerJ 6:e4640 (PMC5922232), full text via Europe PMC
Same dataset, metadata file WBDSinfo.csv (Figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.5722711)

facts.notes: Computed from the dataset's metadata file (script fukuchi_fr.py), 'Young' group, overground comfortable-speed trials (n = 24): speed 1.24 ± 0.14 m/s; leg 0.877 m; stature 1.711 m. Fr = v²/(9.81 L) per person: mean 0.182, sd 0.040, min 0.100, max 0.290; leg/stature 0.513 ± 0.015. Paper: 'Leg length was measured by assessing the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the ipsilateral medial malleolus while the participant lay in a supine position.' That is not hip-joint height. The paper's own dimensionless speed is v/√(g l0); we used Alexander's v²/(gL). Barefoot, lab. Verifier: recomputed, all match. Caveat: speed was timed over a 10 m walkway starting and ending at rest, and the paper warns speeds 'might have been slightly underestimated', so 0.18 is at the low end (CADENCE's 1.34 m/s gives 0.21; Bohannon's ~1.4 m/s about 0.22).
facts.who_when: Data: Fukuchi et al. 2018; computation: this research, 2026

facts.label: Dynamic similarity: Froude number on hip height; human walking duty factor 0.55–0.7
facts.unit_si: duty factor (fraction of stride with the foot down)
facts.display: Duty factor about 0.7 in very slow walking, falling to 0.55 in fast walking; use hip height as the length; step 0.8–1.2 hip heights. (Our working value 0.6 is an estimate, not from the paper)

sources.title: Alexander (2004), Bipedal animals, and their differences from humans, J Anat 204:321 (PMC1571302)

facts.notes: Quotes: 'dynamic similarity is possible only between systems moving at equal Froude numbers, (speed)2/(length × gravitational acceleration).' 'similar animals of different sizes, travelling over land at equal Froude numbers, would tend to move in dynamically similar fashion. Strict dynamic similarity would not be possible, because animals of different sizes are generally not geometrically similar'. 'For our characteristic length, we used the height of the hip joint from the ground in normal standing'. 'Humans use duty factors of about 0.7 in very slow walking, falling to about 0.55 in fast walking'. Step lengths 'in the range 0.8–1.2(hip height)' (distance travelled while one foot is down). Verifier: value_si 0.6 was our chosen midpoint inside a verified fact; set to null, only 0.55–0.7 is verified. The paper gives no walk-to-run Froude number (see Kram 1997).

facts.label: Walk-to-run switch at Froude number about 0.5
facts.display: People (and other bipeds) switch from walking to running at a Froude number of about 0.5

sources.title: Kram, Domingo & Ferris (1997), Effect of reduced gravity on the preferred walk-run transition speed, J Exp Biol 200:821 (PubMed 9076966), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'The ratio of the centripetal and gravitational forces (mv2/L)/(mg) reduces to the dimensionless Froude number (v2/gL). Applying this model to a walking human, m is body mass, v is forward velocity, L is leg length and g is gravity. In normal gravity, humans and other bipeds with different leg lengths all choose to switch from a walk to a run at different absolute speeds but at approximately the same Froude number (0.5).' The inverted-pendulum walk becomes impossible at Fr = 1; people switch earlier, at 0.5. Verifier: quote matches; L is 'leg length', not explicitly hip height, which is close enough for this use.

facts.label: Human stance time at a normal walk (computed)
facts.display: Each foot is down about 0.6 s per step at 1.34 m/s (0.58–0.74 s)

sources.title: Tudor-Locke et al. (2019) CADENCE-adults (cadence at 3.0 mph)
Alexander (2004) J Anat (duty factors)

facts.notes: Stance = duty factor × stride period. Stride period = 2 / step frequency = 2 / (113.6/60) = 1.057 s (step_tudorlocke2019_cadence_vs_speed). Duty factor 0.55–0.7 (step_alexander2004_dynamic_similarity), with 0.6 as the middle; 0.6 is my choice, not measured at this speed. Cross-check: Baines et al. 2018 measured 1.9 Hz steps at 1.3 m/s, the same stride. I fetched no directly measured stance time. Öberg et al. 1993 (J Rehabil Res Dev) failed TLS verification on the VA site, and I did not bypass it.

facts.label: Heel strike in barefoot walking: heel speed, timing, energy absorbed, effective mass
facts.display: At 1.3 m/s the heel lands at 0.57 m/s downward; the impact peaks 17.5 ms after contact; heel strike lasts 30 ms; about 3.8 J absorbed per step

sources.title: Baines, Schwab & van Soest (2018), Experimental estimation of energy absorption during heel strike in human barefoot walking, PLOS ONE 13:e0197428 (PMC6023236), full text via Europe PMC

facts.notes: Table 1: 12 healthy adults (4 men, 8 women), 76.7 ± 15 kg, barefoot, preferred speed, force plate synchronised with Optotrak. 'on average ŻH(t0) = −0.57 m/s and ŻH(tp) = −0.52 m/s'. 'The mechanical energy loss of heel strike is around 3.8 J for preferred walking speeds (≈ 1.3 m/s)'. 'foot mass Me = 11 ± 3% of bodyweight'. Impact-peak size in body weights is only in a figure; heights and leg lengths not reported. Conflicts with Winter 1992. Verifier: Table 1 matches exactly. (a) The 'heel point' is a virtual point fixed to two tibia markers, located from the centre of pressure; no marker on the foot. (b) W is work done by the ground force on the foot and ankle, i.e. energy dissipated or stored in the heel pad, foot and ankle. On a rigid plate essentially none of it enters the ground: it is not energy delivered to the ground.

facts.label: Effective mass stopped at heel strike (older method)
facts.display: 6.3% of body mass in walking (5.3% running, 3.7% crouched walking); 0.24–3.99 J at impact

sources.title: Chi & Schmitt (2005), Mechanical energy and effective foot mass during impact loading of walking and running, J Biomech 38:1387 (PubMed 15922749), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'The magnitude of Meff as a percentage of body mass (M(B)) varies with knee angle at impact and significantly differs among gaits: 6.3%M(B) in walking, 5.3%M(B) in running, and 3.7%M(B) in crouched walking.' and 'At the instant prior to heel strike, Etot ranges from 0.24 to 3.99 J.' Baines et al. 2018 show that this method's assumption (heel speed zero at the impact peak) is not met; with synchronised data they get 11% (to the end of heel strike). Treat 6.3% as a low estimate. Verifier: corrected 'published estimates span 4–18%' to 'Baines et al. 2018 get 4–18% depending on method' (4.1% with this method to 17.6% to the impact peak).

facts.label: Heel speed at contact (older marker study)
facts.display: Heel contact: vertical speed 'negligible', horizontal 0.87 m/s

sources.title: Winter (1992), Foot trajectory in human gait: a precise and multifactorial motor control task, Phys Ther 72:45 (PubMed 1728048), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'Heel-contact velocity was negligible vertically and small (0.87 m/s) horizontally.' 11 subjects, 10 walking trials each. Disputed: Baines et al. 2018 measured 0.57 m/s downward at contact with synchronised high-rate force and motion data. Use Baines for the impact calculation. Why they differ is not established. Verifier: a likely cause is the definitions: Winter tracked a heel marker, while Baines used a tibia-fixed virtual point under the centre of pressure. Our earlier idea that Winter's marker data were smoothed through contact is speculation (full text paywalled, not read).

facts.label: How often a heel-strike transient appears in barefoot walking
facts.display: A sharp heel-strike spike appears in 76% of barefoot walking trials (smooth 13%, none 11%)

sources.title: Verdini et al. (2006), Identification and characterisation of heel strike transient, Gait Posture 23:77 (PubMed 16263287), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'A short-lived sharp HST was present in 76% of the trials while a smooth HST, of longer duration was seen in 13.3% of the trials. The transient phenomenon was absent in the remaining 10.7% of trials.' The size (in body weights) and rise time are not in the abstract, and the full text is paywalled. Whittle 1999 (Gait Posture review) was also not readable.

facts.label: Timing of the heel-strike transient after contact
facts.display: The heel-strike spike peaks 11–16 ms after the foot touches down

sources.title: Blackburn et al. (2016), Comparison of three methods for identifying the heelstrike transient during walking gait, Med Eng Phys 38:581 (PubMed 27118622), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'Twenty-eight healthy subjects walked at a self-selected pace' and 'the Radin and Modified Hunt methods identifying the HST 11-16ms following ground contact and the Hunt method identifying the HST 83-122ms following ground contact.' The 83–122 ms result is a different feature (the loading peak). Consistent with Baines et al. 2018 (impact peak at 17.5 ms, 12–23).

facts.label: Soft-footed walking: how much people cut their footstep impact when asked to walk quietly
facts.unit_si: fractional reduction in impact loading rate
facts.display: Walking quietly cuts the impact loading rate by 45% (heel-first, while walking 29% slower) to 69% (toe- or flat-footed, 23% slower); 49% when asked to keep normal speed

sources.title: Yoon et al. (2025), How to walk to reduce footstep noise in multi-story residential buildings, Ergonomics (PubMed 38186284), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'participants who struck the ground with the rearfoot reduced the impact loading rate by 44.6% with 29.3% slower walking speed than normal walking. Those who struck with the fore- or mid-foot reduced the impact loading by 69.2% with a 23.4% decrease in speed. Quiet walking with the non-rearfoot strike pattern reduced the impact loading by 48.7%, even when asked to walk as fast as normal walking.' 26 young participants. No peak-force change is given; the weight must still be carried. Verifier: quotes match. Part of the 45% and 69% cuts comes from walking slower, so 48.7% at normal speed is the cleaner technique figure. Only loading rate was measured: applying this factor to impact energy (as the recommendation and engine SOFT = 0.4 do) is an estimate, not supported by this study.

facts.label: Peak force of army drill stamps (deliberate straight-leg heel stamp), group means
facts.display: Drill stamps, group means: 3.1–6.6 × body weight (trained men 5.9–6.6, untrained men 3.7–4.6, trained women 3.1–4.1); marching 1.1–1.3. Individuals vary (SD up to 1.7 ×). Rigid floor, army boots

sources.title: Carden et al. (2015), Force and acceleration characteristics of military foot drill: implications for injury risk in recruits, BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med 1:e000025 (PMC5117012), full text via Europe PMC

facts.notes: Table 3. 24 trained soldiers (12 men, 81.5 kg, 180 cm; 12 women, 66.6 kg) and 12 untrained men (70.6 kg), all in Combat Assault Boots, on Kistler plates at 1,000 Hz; peak = 'highest instantaneous vertical ground reaction force'. Technique: 'an exaggerated stamping of one foot into the ground from 90° hip flexion'; 'stamp the heel in to the ground as hard as possible in an attempt to make a ‘loud noise’'; 'all participants impacted the ground with a straight leg'. Contact duration and foot speed not reported. Verifier: tables match. 3.1–6.6 BW is the range of group means, not of individuals: trained men's SD is 1.5–1.7 BW (upper 95% confidence limit about 7.7), so some individuals likely exceeded 8 BW (inferred; individual maxima not reported). Measured on rigid force plates; on soil the peak and loading rate would be lower.

facts.label: Loading rate of army drill stamps
facts.display: Drill stamps load the ground at 316–983 body weights per second (marching 42–70)

sources.title: Carden et al. (2015), BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med (PMC5117012), Table 4

facts.notes: Loading rate was 'calculated as the first derivative of vertical ground reaction and time using finite difference method', taking the largest instantaneous value, with the force filtered at 100 Hz. Discussion: 'the highest loading rate measured by Munro et al11 for running (113 BW/s at 5 m/s) was only around a third of our lowest recorded value.'

facts.label: Time from contact to peak force in drill stamps (the abstract's unit corrected by inference)
facts.display: Drill stamps reach peak force 16–36 ms after contact; peaks above 5 × body weight and 350 body weights per second

sources.title: Rawcliffe et al. (2020), The effects of British Army footwear on ground reaction force and temporal parameters of British Army foot drill, J Strength Cond Res 34:754 (PubMed 28800005), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'the mean of 8 trials from 15 recreationally active men were collected from 4 foot drills' and 'Foot drill produced peak vGRF and peak vertical rate of force development in excess of 5 bw, and 350 bw·s, respectively. Time to peak vGRF ranged from 0.016 to 0.036 ms across foot drills'. The printed 'ms' must be seconds: 0.016 ms would need about 300,000 BW/s, while 5 BW in 0.016–0.036 s averages 140–310 BW/s, which fits. Likewise '350 bw·s' must be bw/s. Three footwear types; the abstract gives no numbers for the difference. value_si is the midpoint of the range (our choice). Verifier: quotes match; status verified with both units corrected by inference. Subjects were recreationally active men, not soldiers.
facts.who_when: Rawcliffe, Graham, Simpson, Moir, Martindale, Psycharakis & Connaboy 2020

facts.label: 60 cm drop landing: peak force
facts.display: Landing from a 60 cm drop: about 3.4 × body weight (as cited by Carden et al.)

sources.title: Carden et al. (2015), citing Decker et al. (2003) Clin Biomech 18:662
Decker et al. (2003) abstract (does not state the force), via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Carden: 'Mean drill manoeuvre peak vertical impact forces for TRAINED men (6.3 BW), women (3.5 BW) and UNTRAINED men (4.2 BW) were 41%, 3% and 13% greater than those reported by Decker et al30 for a 60 cm drop landing (3.4 BW).' Decker's abstract does not give the force, so this is not verified at the source. Physics: a 0.60 m drop lands at √(2gh) = 3.4 m/s. People landing from drops bend their knees; drill stamps are straight-legged, hence the higher loading rates.

facts.display: US Army men (n = 4,082): crotch 0.48, hip (top of thigh bone) 0.51, knee 0.28 of height; thigh about 0.23

facts.label: Rex's and Ollie's hip height (leg length for gait scaling)
facts.display: Hip height about 0.45 of height: 1.37 m (1.28–1.46 m)

sources.title: Owner's turnaround art, front views, measured here: build-comparison/assets/rex-turnaround.png
Owner's turnaround art, front views, measured here: build-comparison/assets/ollie-turnaround.png
ANSUR II men (crotch-to-hip gap, step_ansur_leg_proportions), as stored in this repo

facts.notes: Our own measurement, not published. Rex front view: crest tip y≈13 px, soles y≈750, crotch (lowest point of the briefs between the thighs) y≈445, so the crotch is at 0.414 H. Ollie: horn tips y≈18, soles y≈775, crotch y≈462, so 0.413 H. Adding the human crotch-to-hip gap (0.031 H, ANSUR II) gives 0.445 H for both; 0.45 H × 3.048 m = 1.37 m. The range 0.42–0.48 H covers reading error (±5 px ≈ ±0.007 H) and the hidden hip-joint position inside such massive thighs. The engine already uses Lleg = 0.45 H. Canon heights: Rex 3.048 m to his crest tip; Ollie 3.06 m to his horn tips (corrected from '3.048 m for both'; the 0.4% difference is far inside the range). Verifier: re-measured independently, Rex 0.414 H, Ollie 0.416 H (soles ~778 px). Heel-first, like people, is canon (owners, 12 Oct 2026); the 0.45 H hip height stays our measurement.

facts.label: Rex's and Ollie's comfortable walking pace (people scaled up at equal Froude number)
facts.display: About 1.6–1.7 m/s (about 6 km/h) as a default; 1.2 m/s at Froude 0.1 (slow); 2.0 m/s brisk

sources.title: Fukuchi et al. (2018) dataset (preferred Froude number)
Alexander (2004) J Anat (dynamic similarity)

facts.notes: Computed: v = √(Fr g h), h = 1.37 m (1.28–1.46). Fr 0.18 gives 1.56 m/s (1.50–1.61 across h); Fr 0.10 gives 1.16; Fr 0.29 gives 1.98. Matching CADENCE's 1.34 m/s human (Fr 0.209 on hip height 0.875 m) gives 1.68 m/s. Status estimate (was derived): the hip height is our estimate and human-like gait is assumed, ignoring their bulk, wide stance, boots and personal choice. Verifier: recomputed; it inherits Fukuchi's start-from-rest underestimate, so 1.6–1.7 m/s is a fair default. Keeper-guided elephants walked at Fr 0.05–0.08 (step_elephant_walk_froude_measured); 'elephants self-select Fr about 0.1' is only reported (step_elephant_preferred_froude).

facts.label: Speed where Rex or Ollie would break into a run
facts.display: Walk-to-run switch near 2.6 m/s (9.3 km/h)

sources.title: Kram, Domingo & Ferris (1997) (Fr 0.5)

facts.notes: Computed: v = √(0.5 × 9.81 × h): 2.59 m/s at h = 1.37 m (2.51–2.68 for h = 1.28–1.46). Kram used leg length; the engine should use the same hip height throughout. Status estimate (was derived) because the hip height is our estimate and human-like gait is assumed. Above this, the walking step model (about 1.2 BW) no longer applies; running loads are 2–3 BW (walking_running_peak_vertical_force). Verifier: recomputed, 2.59 m/s (2.51–2.68).

facts.label: Rex's and Ollie's step rate and step length at a comfortable walk
facts.display: About 88–91 steps per minute (1.5 per second), each step about 1.1 m

sources.title: Tudor-Locke et al. (2019) CADENCE-adults (cadence table)

facts.notes: Computed. Dimensionless step rate f̂ = f √(h/g). CADENCE cohort stature 1.707 m, so hip ≈ 0.875 m (ANSUR ratio). At 3.0 mph f̂ = 1.893 × √(0.875/9.81) = 0.566 at Fr 0.209. A power fit over 2.0–4.0 mph gives f̂ = 0.789 Fr^0.211. For h = 1.37 m: Fr 0.209 (1.68 m/s) gives 1.51 Hz (91/min), step 1.11 m; Fr 0.18 (1.56 m/s) gives 1.47 Hz (88/min), step 1.06 m. Equal-Froude scaling makes every time 1.25× the human's (√(1.37/0.875)). Status estimate (was derived): hip height is our estimate and human-like gait is assumed; treadmill data. Verifier: refit reproduces (67, 78, 88, 95, 109 per min), but the fit spans only Fr 0.093–0.372, so the Fr 0.05 and 0.5 rows are extrapolations and must be flagged.

facts.label: How long each of Rex's or Ollie's feet stays down per step
facts.display: About 0.8 s per footfall at a comfortable walk (0.73–0.93 s)

sources.title: Alexander (2004) J Anat (duty factor 0.55–0.7)
Tudor-Locke et al. (2019) CADENCE-adults

facts.notes: Computed: stance = duty factor × 2 / f. At f = 1.47–1.51 Hz the stride is 1.32–1.36 s; duty 0.55–0.7 gives 0.73–0.93 s; 0.6 gives 0.79–0.82 s (the human 0.63 s × 1.25). Status estimate (was derived): hip height is our estimate, human-like gait is assumed, and 0.6 is our chosen duty factor. Verifier: recomputed; stance length 1.56 × 0.82 = 1.28 m = 0.93 hip heights, inside Alexander's 0.8–1.2. Note: the recommendation's linear duty-factor rule (0.7 at Fr 0.05 to 0.55 at Fr 0.4) gives 0.64 and 0.88 s at Fr 0.18, not 0.6 and 0.82 s; pick one. Compare an elephant: 1.5 s for an African elephant's hind foot at 1.2 m/s (step_hutchinson2006_elephant_timing).

facts.label: Load on one foot at each walking step, and pressure under it
facts.display: 35 kN (about 3.6 tonnes-force) per step at 1.2 × body weight; Rex's paw 114 kPa, Ollie's boot 236 kPa

sources.title: Keller et al. (1996) and the existing key walking_running_peak_vertical_force (1.0–1.5 BW)

facts.notes: 1.2 × 3,007 kg × 9.81 = 35.4 kN; range 1.0–1.5 BW (29.5–44.2 kN). Pressure = force / sole area (rex_ollie_picture_build, an estimate from the picture: Rex 0.31 m², Ollie 0.15 m²): Rex 95 / 114 / 143 kPa; Ollie 197 / 236 / 295 kPa at 1.0 / 1.2 / 1.5 BW. These are sole averages; real soles load unevenly (an elephant's local peaks are about twice its average). A walking biped carries its whole weight on one foot at a time. Floor: averaged over its stance, each foot carries 1/(2 × duty factor) of body weight, 0.71–0.91 BW for duty 0.55–0.7 (0.83 at 0.6); the peak must exceed that, so even soft-footed walking cannot drop the peak much below about 0.9–1.0 BW (estimate). Verifier: recomputed; corrected the floor range (the recommendation's '0.85–1.0' was wrong). Review round 1 (data lens): status estimate (was derived): the pressures use the sole areas measured from the picture (an estimate).

facts.label: Heel strike of one of Rex's or Ollie's normal steps: energy absorbed by the foot (a proxy for impact severity, scaled from people)
facts.display: About 80–230 J at each heel strike, over about 20–40 ms (rough; 30–410 J across methods and subjects). Energy absorbed in the foot, not energy sent into the ground

sources.title: Baines et al. (2018) PLOS ONE (human heel strike)

facts.notes: Scaled at equal Froude number, energy goes as M g h. Baines: 3.8 J total, 2.7 J vertical for 76.7 kg; we assumed a 0.90 m hip (not reported), so E/(M g h) = 5.6e-3 total, 4.0e-3 vertical. Rex/Ollie (3,007 kg, h 1.37 m): 228 J total (84–413), 162 J vertical. Second method, ½ m_e v²: heel 0.57 × √(1.37/0.90) = 0.70 m/s (0.48–0.96), m_e 4–18% of M: 31–131 J (83 J at 11%). facts.label: When footprints form at all (track-formation physics)
facts.display: A print forms only when the foot's pressure is near the ground's yield strength: on firmer ground, no print; on much softer ground, the animal gets mired

sources.title: Falkingham, Bates, Margetts & Manning (2011), The 'Goldilocks' effect: preservation bias in vertebrate track assemblages, J R Soc Interface 8:1142 (PubMed 21233145), abstract via Europe PMC API

facts.notes: Abstract: 'Ideal, semi-infinite elastic-plastic substrates displayed a ‘Goldilocks’ quality where only a narrow range of loads could produce tracks, given that small animals failed to indent the substrate, and larger animals would be unable to traverse the area without becoming mired. If a firm subsurface layer is assumed, a more complete assemblage is possible'. A 2014 follow-up (Falkingham, Hage & Bäker, R Soc Open Sci, PMC4448835; abstract read) found that strain hardening and layering widen that range: 'any given substrate can therefore only preserve a range of tracks from those animals which exert an underfoot pressure at approximately the yield strength of the sediment'. No numbers to use.

So failure-based sinking overpredicts about tenfold unless φ is near 40°, and elasticity underpredicts. On the engine's loose sand (37 kPa at 0.1 m², Nq 18.4) the rule sinks a person 0.21 m per step, Rex 0.17 m, Ollie 0.66 m; no measured human print was fetched to test this. Verifier: reproduced; using local or punching shear factors for this sand would make the overprediction worse. facts.notes: Our rule (engine standDepth), replacing D = (p − q0)/(ρ g N_q), which overpredicted the elephant's print about tenfold (step_footprint_model_check). Print: the Walk tab's footprint rule at the standing pressure, d = 18 mm × (p / 350 kPa)^1.27 × (B / 0.274 m), shallower in gravel in proportion to its bearing (step_rex_ollie_footprint_estimate); fitted on 99–350 kPa, extrapolated outside. That is a lower bound only if the forefoot really pressed 350 kPa (Schanz's calibrated model); if the force-plate 181 kPa is right, the evidence supports only about half, and sinking would start sooner. Past q_fail, D = (p − q_fail)/(ρ g N_q), N_q 18.4 (sand) or 64.19 (gravel); continuous at q_fail. Check: the elephant at 350 kPa gives 18 mm (measured 20–26), at 181 kPa 7.8 mm, standing at Schanz's 93 kPa 3.3 mm (model: 4 mm at 99 kPa). Ollie at ten times his density (983 kPa) would plunge 1.7 m on his feet, past his 1.37 m legs, so his underside takes the load and he stops in to his hips (1.37 m). Clay: the Walk tab's rule, depth where min(9, N_c0 × depth factor) × s_u + γ D = p (EM 1110-1-1905 Table 4-7), nothing below the bearing; no measured clay print anchors it. facts.label: Near the step: quasi-static ground velocity from a changing vertical force (Boussinesq)
facts.display: PPV_near = (1 − ν) · (dF/dt)_max / (2π ρ c_s² r) ≈ 0.119 (dF/dt)_max / (ρ c_s² r)

sources.title: Colombero, Kontoe, Foti & Potts (2015) Numerical modelling of wave attenuation through soil, XVI ECSMGE Edinburgh, pp. 3959-3964 (Politecnico di Torino repository)

facts.notes: Static vertical surface displacement at distance r from a vertical point force F on an elastic half-space: u = (1 − ν) F / (2π μ r), μ = ρ c_s² (Boussinesq). When the force changes slowly compared with the wave transit time, the ground follows quasi-statically: v = (1 − ν) Ḟ / (2π μ r). Checks: the low-frequency limit of the full wavenumber integral gives −(1 − ν)/(2π) = −0.1194; the exact time-domain solution gives PPV·r → 0.375 F/(ρ c_s² T) for a Hann pulse and 0.1875 F/(ρ c_s² τ) for a raised-cosine ramp. Valid for r below about 0.4 c_s T (Hann) or 1.1 c_s τ (ramp), and for r more than about twice the footprint radius. Colombero et al. is cited only for listing Pekeris (1955) and Lamb (1904) as the classical point-load solutions; the formula is textbook elasticity. Verifier: limit and both constants reproduced independently; near-to-far crossovers at x = 0.37 (Hann) and 1.07 (ramp).

facts.notes: Surface vertical displacement for a vertical harmonic point force: u_z = (F/2πμ) ∫ k_s² ν_α k J0(kr) / R(k) dk, with R(k) the Rayleigh function. The Rayleigh pole gives |u_z| = (F/μ) C1 √(k_s / (2π ξ_R r)), ξ_R = c_s/c_R. For ν = 1/4: ξ_R = 1.08766 (c_R = 0.9194 c_s), C1 = 0.19957; velocity = ω u gives 0.19957/√(2π·1.08766) = 0.0763. Checks: (1) the Rayleigh power from this amplitude is 0.04989 ω²F²/(ρ c_s³), against Miller & Pursey's 67.35% × 1.209/(π·3^1.5) = 0.04988; (2) C1 equals √(3√3 + 5)/16, the Rayleigh coefficient in Pekeris's closed form; (3) horizontal/vertical comes out 0.681, the textbook value for ν = 1/4. The ω^1.5 growth is why the quick parts of a footfall dominate far away. Other Poisson ratios in values_json. facts.label: Recommended PPV model for one footfall: exact elastic result for a smooth force pulse, in closed form
facts.display: PPV = max(near, far) × D; Hann pulse of peak F, length T: near = 0.375 F/(ρ c_s² T r), far = 0.620 F/(ρ c_s^2.5 T^1.5 √r); ramp of rise time τ: near = 0.1875 F/(ρ c_s² τ r), far = 0.181 F/(ρ c_s^2.5 τ^1.5 √r)

sources.title: Sanchez-Sesma, Weaver, Kawase, Matsushima, Luzon & Campillo (2011) Energy partitions among elastic waves for dynamic surface loads in a semi-infinite solid, BSSA (accepted manuscript)
Colombero, Kontoe, Foti & Potts (2015) Numerical modelling of wave attenuation through soil, XVI ECSMGE Edinburgh, pp. 3959-3964 (Politecnico di Torino repository)

facts.notes: Vertical surface PPV at distance r from a vertical force on an elastic half-space (ρ, c_s, ν = 1/4). Hann: F·½(1 − cos 2πt/T), 0 ≤ t ≤ T (stamp). Ramp: F·½(1 − cos πt/τ) to τ, then held (footstep; toe-off mirrors it). Exact PPV = F/(ρ c_s³ T²)·Π(x), x = r/(c_s T), with τ for T for the ramp; Π in values_json. max(near, far) is within about 17% of it. D: vib_physics_damping_factor. Assumes uniform ground, footprint radius below 0.2 c_s T, linear ground (vib_linear_strain_limit), vertical force. Verifier: all constants reproduced; table error up to 7%. Checked against data only to 60 m, at one drop site (within about 2×). Beyond about 60 m the damped Hann pulse falls as r^-2 to r^-3, steeper than any measured trend (r^-1.0 to -1.6), so stamps are probably under-predicted there. PPV rises with F at fixed T and falls with r; it is not monotone in T (a longer Hann pulse gives more PPV at 100 m and beyond).

facts.label: Material damping of a footfall pulse with distance (constant damping ratio ξ applied to every frequency)

sources.title: Colombero, Kontoe, Foti & Potts (2015) Numerical modelling of wave attenuation through soil, XVI ECSMGE Edinburgh, pp. 3959-3964 (Politecnico di Torino repository)
Caltrans (2020) Transportation and Construction Vibration Guidance Manual, April 2020 (Andrews, Buehler, Gill & Bender)

facts.notes: Each frequency ω decays as exp(−ω ξ r / c_R) (constant-Q damping; Colombero et al. use the same exp(−2πξ r/λ_R) form, eq. 2). Applied to the far-field Rayleigh pulse spectrum, taking the new peak gives D(ζ), ζ = ξ r/(c_R T). The fits are within a factor of 1.08 (Hann) and 1.20 (ramp) of the computed D over ζ = 0.001–100. At large ζ, D falls as ζ^-2.5 (Hann) or ζ^-1.5 (ramp). One fixed α (Bornitz) applied to the peak over-damps a pulse at long range. D is applied to both near and far terms. Pisa example (ξ 0.03, r 60 m, c_R 138 m/s, T 0.03 s): ζ = 0.43, D = 0.12. Verifier: reproduced by FFT. Caveat: with constant ξ, Hann-pulse PPV on soft ground falls as about r^-2 to r^-3 beyond 30 m (local slope 2.1 at 35–60 m and 2.7 at 100–200 m for Pisa inputs), while measured impact trends are r^-1.0 to -1.6. The ramp is less affected (slope 1.3–1.5).

facts.label: Seismic energy radiated by a changing vertical force on the ground
facts.unit_si: 1 (coefficient in E = k ∫(dF/dt)² dt / (ρ c_s³), ν = 1/4)
facts.display: E_seismic = 2.418/(π ρ c_p³) ∫ (dF/dt)² dt = 0.148 ∫ (dF/dt)² dt / (ρ c_s³); two-thirds of it in Rayleigh waves

sources.title: Sanchez-Sesma, Weaver, Kawase, Matsushima, Luzon & Campillo (2011) Energy partitions among elastic waves for dynamic surface loads in a semi-infinite solid, BSSA (accepted manuscript)

facts.notes: From Π = 1.209 ω² P²/(π ρ c_p³) for P cos ωt, the real part of the ground's point admittance is 2.418 ω²/(π ρ c_p³). For a transient force, Parseval gives E = 2.418/(π ρ c_p³) · ∫ Ḟ² dt; with c_p = √3 c_s this is 0.148 ∫Ḟ² dt/(ρ c_s³). Valid for ν = 1/4 only. Examples (ours): Pisa drop as a 0.025–0.04 s Hann pulse of momentum 997 kg·m/s on c_s = 160 m/s: 6–25 J, 0.2–0.6% of the 3.8 kJ drop energy, above the 10⁻⁴ seismic efficiency the lab uses for large impacts (seismic_efficiency_impact). Rex walking with placeholder inputs (1.2 × body weight, 0.1 s raised-cosine rise and fall): about 1.7 J per step on loose sand, 0.15 J on stiff clay, 6 × 10⁻⁵ J on granite. The energy depends on how fast the force changes, not on body energy, so a seismic-efficiency factor is the wrong tool for footsteps. Verifier: derivation and all examples recomputed.

facts.label: Vertical vs resultant PPV for a footfall
facts.display: Resultant (vector) PPV ≈ 1.0–1.2 × the vertical PPV the model gives, for uniform ground; in the field the vertical is often not the largest component, so the ratio can be higher

sources.title: BS 5228-2:2009+A1:2014 Annex E, Tables E.1 and E.2 (licensed copy filed as public-inquiry core document CD43.12, Omega West)
Hiller & Crabb (2000) TRL Report 429, Groundborne vibration caused by mechanised construction works (Transport Research Laboratory for the Highways Agency)

facts.notes: Rayleigh wave at ν = 1/4: horizontal/vertical amplitude 0.68, a quarter cycle apart, so the resultant peak is close to the vertical peak. Quasi-static near field: radial/vertical surface displacement = (1 − 2ν)/(2(1 − ν)) = 1/3 at ν = 1/4, resultant 1.05 × vertical. BS 5228-2 Table E.1 predicts the resultant ('νres resultant PPV'); some damage standards use the largest single component. Treat model PPV × 1.1 as resultant. Verifier: 0.681 and 1/3 (resultant 1.054) confirmed, but they hold for a uniform half-space. TRL 429 notes from field data that the vertical component 'is often not the largest component', so field resultant/vertical can exceed 1.2.

facts.label: Seismic wave speeds in ice (polar ice sheets)
facts.display: Shear waves 1,934–1,960 m/s; P waves 3,795 − 2.30·T m/s (T in °C); Poisson ratio about 0.33

sources.title: Kohnen (1974) The temperature dependence of seismic waves in ice, Journal of Glaciology 13(67):144-147

facts.notes: Kohnen eq. (1): 'Vp = −(2·30 ± 0.17) T + 3795 m/s'. Table II lists measured Vs of 1934–1960 m/s at −16.5 to −29 °C and Poisson's ratio 0.327–0.332; 'Assuming a constant Poisson's ratio of 0.329'. dVs/dT = −1.2 m/s per degree, so near 0 °C about 1,915–1,920 m/s (our extrapolation). facts.label: Lake ice and steel deck: the ground-wave model does not apply
facts.display: Not modelled: on floating ice or a supported steel deck the step excites plate bending waves, not ground waves

sources.title: Kohnen (1974) The temperature dependence of seismic waves in ice, Journal of Glaciology 13(67):144-147

facts.notes: The model assumes a deep solid half-space. Thick lake ice floats on water: a step makes the sheet bend and sends flexural-gravity waves through it, with spreading, dispersion and damping set by ice thickness and water depth. A steel deck plate rests on beams: the response is the deck's own resonances. Neither was researched in this run. Recommended page wording: 'Ground shaking is not modelled on lake ice or a steel deck (they flex as plates).' The bulk speeds (ice c_s about 1.9 km/s, Kohnen 1974; steel about 3.2 km/s, estimate) are listed for reference only.

facts.label: How far the dynamic-compaction laws are being stretched for footsteps
facts.unit_si: ratio (BS 5228 lower energy limit / smallest footstep energy)
facts.display: Footsteps (our assumed 10 J–10 kJ) sit 100 to 100,000 times below BS 5228's 1 MJ floor. At 82 kJ the law already under-predicts 1.4–5× within 30 m and 2.5–10× at 50–100 m; at 3.8 kJ about 5× at 60 m. Walking is a slow load, not a drop, so an energy law has no clear input

sources.title: BS 5228-2:2009+A1:2014 Annex E, Tables E.1 and E.2 (licensed copy filed as public-inquiry core document CD43.12, Omega West)
Hiller & Crabb (2000) TRL Report 429, Groundborne vibration caused by mechanised construction works (Transport Research Laboratory for the Highways Agency)
Colombero, Kontoe, Foti & Potts (2015) Numerical modelling of wave attenuation through soil, XVI ECSMGE Edinburgh, pp. 3959-3964 (Politecnico di Torino repository)
Lukas (1995) Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 1: Dynamic Compaction, FHWA-SA-95-037 (USDOT ROSAP scan)

facts.notes: Ranges: BS 5228-2 dynamic compaction 1–12 MJ and 5–100 m; GEC 1 chart lines at a scaled energy factor of about 0.07–6 √(t·m)/m (our reading); a 10 J–10 kJ footstep at 1–200 m gives about 0.0002–1. The 10 J–10 kJ footstep energy is our assumed range, not a verified input. Below the range: at 82 kJ (TRL 429, Allen 1996) measured PPV was 1.4–5× the Mayne (1985) value within 30 m and 2.5–10× at 50–100 m; at 3.8 kJ (Pisa) the law agrees at 2.5 m and is about 5× low at 60 m; no drop data found at 10 J–1 kJ. At low energy the measured fall-off (r^-1.1 to r^-1.35) is slower than the law's r^-1.7, so errors grow with distance. A walking step loads the ground over roughly 0.1–0.3 s with no free fall; its shaking depends on force and loading rate (vib_physics_pulse_ppv_model). Verifier: status lowered from derived to estimate; 82 kJ ratios corrected from 2–10×.

facts.label: Where the elastic model stops: ground strain near a heavy step
facts.display: Flag results where max(PPV/c_s, (1 − ν)F/(2π ρ c_s² r²)) is above about 10⁻⁴. The limit is an unsourced working value (for sands the linear threshold may be nearer 10⁻⁵), and near the foot the model error could go either way

sources.title: Colombero, Kontoe, Foti & Potts (2015) Numerical modelling of wave attenuation through soil, XVI ECSMGE Edinburgh, pp. 3959-3964 (Politecnico di Torino repository)

facts.notes: Wave strain is about particle velocity / wave speed. Near the foot the strain is quasi-static, (1 − ν)F/(2π μ r²) with μ = ρ c_s², larger than PPV/c_s by about 2 c_s τ/(π r) for a ramp. For a normal step (1.2 × 3,007 kg × g = 35.4 kN) on loose sand it is 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ at 1 m (7.6 × PPV/c_s) and 4.6 × 10⁻⁵ at 2 m, so ordinary walking passes 10⁻⁴ within about 1.4 m. Soil stiffness falls and damping rises from somewhere around 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ strain, and soils yield near 10⁻³ (typical soil-dynamics ranges; no source fetched). Where the flag trips, the direction of the model error is unknown: yielding absorbs energy, but softening raises quasi-static motion (u ∝ 1/μ). Pisa: 9 mm/s at 2.5 m on 150 m/s ground is 6 × 10⁻⁵ wave strain. Verifier: the flag now includes the quasi-static strain; the earlier claim that the model over-estimates close in is withdrawn.

facts.label: Walking: the other foot unloading partly cancels the far-field shaking
facts.unit_si: factor (possible reduction, far field, walking only)
facts.display: While one foot loads, the other unloads; at distances and wavelengths much larger than the stride, the net force changes less, so walking PPV far away may be up to about 2× lower than a single-foot calculation

sources.title: Ekimov & Sabatier (2006) Vibration and sound signatures of human footsteps in buildings, J Acoust Soc Am 120(2):762-8 (PubMed abstract, PMID 16938964, via NCBI E-utilities)

facts.notes: The ground sees the sum of both feet's forces. While each foot alone goes from zero to 1.0–1.5 × body weight, the sum of both feet in walking varies much less, because one foot unloads as the other loads (general walking biomechanics, not from the cited abstract; Ekimov & Sabatier only note that the force of multiple footsteps is concentrated at 1–4 Hz). For wavelengths long compared with Rex's stride (1–2 m) the loading and unloading feet act partly as one varying source, which lowers the far-field PPV; near either foot (r of a few metres or less) the nearer foot dominates and the single-foot result holds. Fast transients (foot slap at touchdown) do not cancel. Not quantified with data; treat the single-foot model as an upper estimate for walking.

facts.display: Largest step about 4 × 10⁻⁸ m (40 nanometres); a typical step about 2 × 10⁻⁸ m

sources.title: Steinmann, Nissen-Meyer, Cotton, Tilmann & Mortimer (2025) Decoding the footsteps of the African savanna: classifying wildlife using seismic signals and machine learning. Methods Ecol. Evol. 16(4):819-836, doi:10.1111/2041-210X.70021 (published version, GFZ repository)

Largest peak +4.0e-8 m (minimum −3.1e-8); median of the 12 largest peaks 1.9e-8 m; reading error about ±0.1e-8. Station NWP05 'is located on sandy dry ground'; data 'at 200 Hz ... high-pass filtered with a 5 Hz corner frequency'. The 20 m is a camera-trap estimate. The paper says only 'broadband seismometers' and does not describe instrument correction. Reported (secondary): Wijayaraja et al. 2024 say Szenicer et al., whose SeisSavanna data these are, used a Guralp 6TD seismometer. Verifier: own reading 3.9e-8 m max, 1.85e-8 m typical.

facts.label: Walking African bush elephant 20 m away: peak vertical ground velocity (converted from displacement)

sources.title: Steinmann et al. (2025) Methods Ecol. Evol. 16:819-836, Fig. 3f (published version, GFZ repository)

facts.notes: Formula: peak velocity ≈ 2πf × peak displacement, treating each footfall as a narrow-band wavelet at its dominant frequency. Inputs: 4.0e-8 m (largest step) and 1.9e-8 m (typical) from elephant_steinmann2025_walk_20m_displacement; f = 18.7 Hz from elephant_steinmann2025_footfall_frequency. Largest step 2π × 18.7 × 4.0e-8 = 4.7e-6 m/s; typical 2.2e-6; over the 13.8–24.3 Hz quartiles the largest step gives 3.5e-6 to 6.1e-6. Expect ±30–50% from the conversion. Vertical component only. Verifier: own reading gives 4.5e-6 m/s (3.3–5.8e-6). Verifier corrected the vector caveat: for an ideal Rayleigh wave the true vector peak equals the vertical peak; only a pseudo-vector sum of separate component peaks is about 1.2×. Real horizontal/vertical ratios on soft ground were not measured. Best single anchor: the only peer-reviewed record in physical units of a walking elephant at a stated distance. Still one animal, one site, one record.

facts.label: Elephant footfalls lack the sharp impulses of hoofed animals (authors link this to soft cushion-like feet); separately, the elephant gave smaller amplitudes than a giraffe, which the authors call surprising
facts.display: No sharp impulses, which the authors link to 'soft cushion-like feet'; smaller amplitudes than a giraffe and similar to a more distant zebra, which they call 'surprising' and do not explain

sources.title: Steinmann et al. (2025) Methods Ecol. Evol. 16:819-836 (GFZ repository)

facts.notes: Quotes: 'While hoofed animals such as giraffes, zebras and warthogs produce clear and sharp impulses (Figure 3a,b,e), elephant with its soft cushion-like feet and hyena with its paws do not show these clear impulses (Figure 3d,f).' 'It is surprising to see that the elephant, having the largest average weight compared to the other animals, produces smaller amplitudes than the giraffe and similar amplitudes to the zebra, which is even more distant.' The authors link the feet only to the impulse shape. That the cushioned feet also explain the weaker amplitude is our inference, not theirs; if it holds, seismic output depends on how sharply the foot lands, not only on mass. Verifier: the earlier label and summary had attributed the weaker signal to the feet; relabelled.

facts.display: 87% balanced accuracy up to 50 m; 77% up to 150 m (150 m is where the dataset stops, not a detection limit)

sources.title: Steinmann et al. (2025) Methods Ecol. Evol. 16:819-836 (GFZ repository)
Steinmann et al., EGU General Assembly 2025 abstract EGU25-2842

facts.notes: Quote: 'The machine learning model achieves a balanced accuracy of 87% with a maximum animal-sensor distance of 50 m and 77% with a maximum animal-sensor distance of 150 m'. The authors put the drop down to 'decreasing signal and label quality'. Seismograms 'were extracted from seismic stations that are not further away than 150 m from the localized animals', so 150 m is the maximum distance chosen when building the dataset, not a measured detection or noise limit. SeisSavanna: 70,637 three-component 10 s seismograms from 11 wildlife categories. Classification by a broadband seismometer, not a range at which people could feel anything. facts.label: Elephant step: seismic-band source force as a share of body weight
facts.display: Adult walks about 0.4–4% of body weight; a climbing step 3.5–5% (if the elephants weighed 2.5–3.5 t)

sources.title: Mortimer et al. (2018) Supplemental Table S1 (forces)
Ren & Hutchinson (2008) J. R. Soc. Interface 5:195-211, Table 1 (masses of comparable elephants)

facts.notes: Formula: F_seis / (m g). The Kenyan elephants were not weighed; we assumed 2,500–3,500 kg (as elephant_ren2008_masses). The assumption fits only the adult walks: Walks 2 and 5 were young animals and are left out. Adult walks: 125 N → 0.36–0.51%; 279 N → 0.8–1.1%; 946 N (fast walk) → 2.8–3.9%. Climbing step 1,190 N → 3.5–4.9%. Heavier adult bulls would give smaller shares. Use: an elephant-like soft step puts only a few percent of body weight into the band that makes ground vibration. Feeding the full ground reaction force (1.2 × body weight, W8.WALK_LOAD) into a seismic formula would overstate it by about 30–300×. Verifier: arithmetic confirmed; corrected 30–200× to 30–300× and restricted the mass assumption to the adult walks.

facts.display: Mean 0.276 µm/s at 10 m (40–60 Hz band; RMS by context); not directly comparable with stomp peak values

sources.title: O'Connell-Rodwell et al. (2006) Wild elephant (Loxodonta africana) breeding herds respond to artificially transmitted seismic stimuli. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 59:842-850 (author PDF, UCLA)

facts.notes: Quote: playback was raised 'to peak presentation velocities ranging from 0.44 to 1.1 μm/s root mean square (RMS) at 10 m from the elephants, approximating the velocity of a naturally occurring seismic elephant rumble (40–60 Hz) at this distance (mean 0.276 μm/s; O'Connell-Rodwell et al. 2000a)'. The paper does not explicitly call the 0.276 mean RMS; the sentence implies it. The 2024 secondary quote gives 0.437 µm/s RMS at 3–12 m and 0.264 at 40 m for rumbles. Band-limited RMS values are not peak values. Mortimer 2018 found large rumble source forces (up to 2,546 N), so the studies differ on rumbles. Verifier: removed the earlier '100× weaker than a stomp' comparison, which set an RMS value against a peak value.

facts.label: Measured surface-wave attenuation fitted near an elephant waterhole (Etosha calcrete, 40–60 Hz)
facts.display: L = L0 · e^(−αr) / √r, with α = 0.018 per m (elephant-generated background) to 0.05 per m (buried shakers)

sources.title: O'Connell-Rodwell et al. (2006) Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 59:842-850, Eq. 1 and Table 1 (author PDF, UCLA)

facts.notes: Quotes: 'we used the standard surface wave attenuation rate model (White 1965)'; Eq. (1) 'relates the velocity level L (m/s) at distance r based on a source signal level L0 and propagation constant α'. Fits: 'α=0.05/m and L0=25.5×10−6 m3/2/s ... for shaker-induced motions'; background 'α=0.018/m and L0=4×10−7 m3/2/s'. Table 1 noise α per trial 0.007–0.023 (mean 0.016). Ground: 'relatively homogeneous calcrete' (Etosha). Fitted at 40–60 Hz (45 Hz shakers) from two geophones (10 m and 90 m). Verifier: recomputed Eq. 1 (13.8 dB at 10 m, −30.5 dB at 90 m, as printed). Do not carry α to footstep frequencies near 20 Hz without scaling: at constant Q, α scales with f, giving roughly 0.008–0.022 per m at 20 Hz (verifier's scaling, an estimate). Using 0.05 per m at 20 Hz would cut 100 m amplitudes by e^−5 (about 150-fold) on top of spreading.

facts.label: Seismic background near a busy elephant waterhole (Etosha, 40–60 Hz band): measured at two geophones and modelled at the elephants
facts.display: −12 dB re 1 µm/s (about 0.25 µm/s) at the elephants, 5 m from the waterhole; −20 dB (0.1 µm/s) and −42 dB (0.008 µm/s) at the geophones 10 m and 90 m from the shakers. Band levels, not footfall peaks

sources.title: O'Connell-Rodwell et al. (2006) Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 59:842-850, Table 1 and Results (author PDF, UCLA)

facts.notes: From the verifier's list. Results: 'the mean background activity level is −12 dB re 1 μm/s for an overall SNR at the location of the elephants of −1.6 dB'. Table 1 means over eight trials: noise level −20.1 dB (SD 4.7) at the 10 m geophone and −42.1 dB (SD 5.1) at the 90 m geophone; −12.0 dB (SD 5.0) at the elephants, calculated with Eq. (1) at 'body length or 5 m from the water hole'. Conversion 10^(dB/20) µm/s: 0.25, 0.099 and 0.0079 µm/s (verifier confirmed −12 dB = 0.251). The authors assumed the noise came from the elephants at the waterhole, 'as their footfalls create seismic noise'. These are 40–60 Hz band levels (RMS by context), not single-step peaks, so they cannot be set directly against peak footfall values. One site (calcrete).

facts.label: Range at which a single geophone picked up elephant footfalls at an Etosha waterhole
facts.display: About 100 m

sources.title: Wood, O'Connell-Rodwell & Klemperer (2005) Using seismic sensors to detect elephants and other large mammals: a potential census technique. J. Appl. Ecol. 42:587-594 (Stanford CRUSTAL PDF)

facts.notes: Quote: 'Given that the duration of the recording in which footfalls are visible is 166 s, the radius of detection is roughly 100 m.' Speed: 'we estimated its speed at 1·2 m s−1'. Discussion: 'the detection radius for an elephant footfall is roughly 100 m in Etosha National Park. This will vary depending on the soil type'. Setup: 'a single 4·5 Hz vertical geophone ... buried 1 m from a major path leading to the waterhole, at a depth of 15 cm'; 31 bull and 12 herd recordings at Mushara waterhole, June 2002. Amplitudes normalized only. Wild African elephants, masses not given. The only measured detection radius among these studies; it is site-specific (the other long ranges are dataset cut-offs, space limits or models).

facts.label: How much weaker a bull's footfalls were at 20 m than directly over the geophone
facts.display: About 20 dB (×10 in amplitude) weaker at 20 m

sources.title: Wood et al. (2005) J. Appl. Ecol. 42:587-594, Fig. 4 and text (Stanford CRUSTAL PDF)

facts.notes: Quote: 'we can use Fig. 4 to estimate the maximum amplitude for an elephant that passed 20 m from the geophone. As indicated on the figure, this is considerably lower (∼20 dB) than when the elephant passed directly over the geophone.' 20 dB = ×10 in amplitude. The geophone was buried 1 m from the path, so 'directly over' is about 1 m, giving a decay exponent n = ln 10 / ln(20/1) ≈ 0.77; n = 1.0 would need r0 = 2 m (verifier). The authors' estimate from a time-to-distance conversion of one bull's envelope, not a calibrated pair of measurements.

facts.display: Most energy 10–40 Hz, peak near 25 Hz; a front-foot strike about every 1.5 s at 1.2 m/s

facts.notes: Quotes: 'All species have a peak around 25 Hz but the shape of the spectra are different, with the elephant spectrum having the most pronounced low-frequency component'. sources.title: Wijayaraja et al. (2024) arXiv 2406.05140, Figs 18a and 21 (gain S0 = 580)

facts.notes: Formula: v = counts × ADC step / (gain × geophone sensitivity). Inputs stated in the paper: 10-bit ADC 'with a resolution of 4.88 mV'; gain 580 (S0); sensitivity 85.8 V/(m/s). facts.label: How fast elephant footfall vibration falls with distance: exponent n in PPV ∝ D^−n, from the elephant studies
facts.display: n about 1 (0.4–2): halving the distance roughly doubles the vibration

sources.title: Wood et al. (2005) J. Appl. Ecol. 42:587-594
Wijayaraja et al. (2024) arXiv 2406.05140 (quoting O'Connell-Rodwell 2000)
Steinmann et al. (2025) Fig. 4b,c (GFZ repository)

facts.notes: Formula: n = ln(A1/A2) / ln(D2/D1). (1) O'Connell-Rodwell stomps (reported, secondary): 24.4 → 8.5 µm/s from '3–12 m' to 40 m gives n = 0.41 (D1 = 3), 0.55 (6), 0.87 (12). (2) Wood: ×10 from 'directly over' (about 1 m) to 20 m gives n ≈ 0.77 (1.0 if 2 m). (3) Steinmann giraffes at ETA00, 26 → 103 m: n = 2.0, probably steepened by the far trace sitting near the noise floor, possibly different animals. Verifier: O'Connell 2006's fitted law gives effective n of 1.2 (background) to 2.3 (shakers) between 10 and 90 m at 40–60 Hz, about 0.8–1.3 if scaled to 20 Hz; Mortimer's model suggests a shallower decay (near 0.5) for low-frequency, high-force steps on sand (elephant_mortimer2018_modelled_200m). n = 1 for 5–100 m is our judgement over mixed-quality inputs, so the status is 'estimate', not 'derived'.

facts.label: Physics check: ground velocity from a footfall-sized force on an elastic half-space
facts.display: With Mortimer's 125–946 N forces at 20 Hz, at 20 m: about 0.002–0.01 mm/s on firmer soil, 0.01–0.09 mm/s on loose sand, about 0.001 mm/s on soft rock for 946 N (simple elastic-ground model; not valid within about one wavelength)

sources.title: Mortimer et al. (2018) Supplemental Table S1 (source forces used as inputs)

facts.notes: Lamb's problem, Rayleigh-wave far field of a vertical harmonic point force F on a Poisson half-space (ν = 0.25): u_z(r) = (F k_s / (2μ)) × 0.1996 × sqrt(2 / (π k_R r)), k_s = 2πf/Vs, μ = ρVs², k_R = k_s/0.9194; v = 2πf u_z. Static limit checks against Boussinesq. At 20 Hz and 20 m: loose sand (ρ 1,700, Vs 120 m/s) 946 N → 0.085 mm/s, 125 N → 0.011; firmer soil (ρ 1,900, Vs 250) 0.012 and 0.0016; soft rock (Vs 600) 946 N → 0.0012. Soil values are assumed, not sourced. Ignores damping, layering, foot size and the near field: invalid within about one wavelength (6 m at Vs 120, 12.5 m at Vs 250, 30 m at Vs 600). Verifier: formula and all values reproduce; high_si cut from the 2 m sand value (0.27 mm/s, inside one wavelength) to 20 m. At the fast walk's 5–10 Hz band the model gives 0.06–0.09 mm/s at 2 m, so it matches Mortimer's 0.2–0.36 mm/s only within a factor of a few.

facts.label: Caltrans 2020: which sources count as transient and which as continuous
facts.display: Transient = a single isolated event (blasting, drop balls); continuous/frequent intermittent = repeated impacts or vibratory plant (impact pile drivers, compactors)

sources.title: Caltrans (2020) Transportation and Construction Vibration Guidance Manual, CT-HWANP-RT-20-365.01.01 (April 2020)

facts.notes: Caltrans 2020 section 7.3 (p. 37): 'it is apparent that damage thresholds for continuous sources are less than those for single-event or transient sources ... many types of construction activities fall between a single event and a continuous source. An impact pile driver, for example, continuously generates single transient events. As a practical matter ... the criteria can only be reasonably separated into two categories: continuous and transient.' And: 'This synthesis of criteria essentially assumes that the threshold for continuous sources is about half of the threshold for transient sources.' Relevance: a single stomp is like a drop ball (transient); a walk past is a train of impacts, closer to an impact pile driver (continuous/frequent intermittent). That mapping is my reading, not Caltrans's.

facts.notes: FTA 2018 p. 113: 'The background vibration velocity level in residential areas is usually 50 VdB or lower, and the threshold of perception for humans is approximately 65 VdB. A vibration level of 85 VdB in a residence can result in strong annoyance.' Table 5-5 (p. 120) gives the 65/75/85 VdB rows. p. 118: annoyance is 'well below the damage risk threshold for typical buildings (100 VdB)'. VdB = 20 log10(v_rms / 1e-6 in/s) (Eq. 5-1). Table 6-2: frequent means more than 70 events a day, occasional 30-70, infrequent fewer than 30 (Caltrans 2020 Table 8's note misprints 'fewer than 70').

facts.notes: FTA 2018 footnote viii (p. 111): 'The ratio of PPV to maximum rms amplitude is defined as the crest factor for the signal. The crest factor is typically greater than 1.41, although a crest factor of 8 or more is not unusual for impulsive signals. For ground-borne vibration from trains, the crest factor is usually 4 to 5.' Section 7.2 (p. 185): 'The approximate rms vibration velocity levels were calculated from the PPV limits using a crest factor of 4.' facts.notes: Formula: PPV = a / (2 pi f) for a sinusoid, with a = the MMI IV PGA band (Wald 1999: 1.4-3.9 %g = 0.137-0.383 m/s^2) and f the step's dominant frequency. At 20 Hz: 1.09-3.04 mm/s. Assumptions: f, pending the attenuation research; and that rattling follows a fixed acceleration, carried from horizontal, indoor, building-amplified earthquake shaking at about 2 Hz to a short vertical footstep pulse. Wald et al. say low intensities follow acceleration; ISO 2631 (via Caltrans) says people respond to velocity at 8-80 Hz. Ignores duration, building resonance (midwalls up to 4x at 10-25 Hz, RI 8507) and ground versus indoor floor. Verifier: downgraded from derived; the match of the felt/not-felt edge with BS 5228-2's 0.14 mm/s at 20 Hz is coincidental, not a validation (at 40 Hz the method gives 0.07 mm/s); JMA 3-4 is not equivalent to MMI IV.

facts.label: Ground velocity at which a vertical shake exceeds 1 g, so loose objects hop and feet are unloaded (our derivation)
facts.display: PPV = g / (2 pi f): 156 mm/s at 10 Hz, 78 mm/s at 20 Hz, 52 mm/s at 30 Hz, 39 mm/s at 40 Hz

sources.title: Wald et al., ShakeMap Manual, USGS Techniques and Methods 12-A1 (version 1.0, 2006), section 2.5 and Figure 2.5 (reproduces Wald, Quitoriano, Heaton & Kanamori 1999, Earthquake Spectra 15(3):557-564)

facts.notes: Physics, not a published threshold: for sinusoidal vertical motion of velocity amplitude v, peak acceleration is 2 pi f v; when the downward acceleration exceeds g = 9.80665 m/s^2, an unattached object, or a standing person's feet, briefly loses contact with the ground. v = 9.80665 / (2 pi f). So it is a marker for footing as well as for objects; no source here tests people under vertical motion above 1 g. A fixed PPV cannot cover both earthquakes (about 2 Hz, where 1 g needs 780 mm/s) and footsteps (higher). Objects slide sideways at lower acceleration (friction coefficient times g). The USGS source is listed only for the frequency context; the formula is standard kinematics. Verifier recomputed all values.

facts.notes: RI 8507 Conclusion 6 (p. 68): 'Practical safe criteria for blasts that generate low-frequency ground vibrations are 0.75 in/sec for modern gypsumboard houses and 0.50 in/sec for plaster on lath interiors. Abstract: 'Threshold damage was defined as the occurrence of cosmetic damage; that is, the most superficial interior cracking of the type that develops in all homes independent of blasting.' Conclusion 8: below 0.5 in/sec the chance of damage 'is not only small (5 pct for worst cases) but decreases more rapidly than the mean prediction'. Conclusion 7: there may be 'no absolute minimum vibration damage threshold'. Restated in Caltrans 2020 section 11.4.3.1. Data: 219 blasts at 76 homes plus nine earlier studies. Verifier: these are safe levels, not where cracking begins.

facts.display: Standing subjects: some lost balance at the lowest velocity tested at 0.3-0.6 Hz (0.265 m/s) and at 0.32 m/s at 1-2.5 Hz, where 0.13-0.16 m/s caused none. sources.title: Takahashi, Saito, Azuhata & Ohtomo (2004) Shaking table test on indoor human response and evacuation action limit in strong ground motion, 13th World Conference on Earthquake Engineering, Paper 1320

facts.notes: Takahashi et al. 2004, Table 1 (horizontal input sine waves, front-rear and right-left) and Figure 8 'Unbalanced ratio in standing', read from page images (about +-0.05 m/s). Balance was judged by the authors from motion-capture records. Text: 'high frequency motion causes strong anxiousness and low frequency motion causes stagger even if anxiousness is small.' Conclusion: 'additional tests might be need to clarify its limit value' and 'The authors have not find clear limit value for evacuation limit ... because of limitation of number of subjects.' The paper's menisci were pinned at the rim and set by fill volume, not by the wall's contact angle. Inference (not tested in the paper): a cup whose contact angle is near 90° (polystyrene, meniscus about 0.1 mm) should ring weakly; a polypropylene cup's depressed meniscus should still make rings. facts.label: A push spread through a body in proportion to its mass accelerates it with no internal stress
facts.display: If every kilogram gets the same push (b = a everywhere) and nothing touches the surface, stress = 0

sources.title: A. F. Bower, Applied Mechanics of Solids, §2.3.1 Linear momentum balance in terms of Cauchy stress (online text)
NASA EG-1997-08-110-HQ, Microgravity: A Teacher's Guide with Activities in Science, Mathematics, and Technology (Rogers, Vogt & Wargo 1997), PDF pp. 14 and 17

facts.notes: Derived from comic_cauchy_equation_of_motion. Body force per unit mass b = g + f/m, the same at every point (his push in proportion to mass), so the body accelerates uniformly at a = b. σ = 0 then satisfies ∇·σ + ρb = ρa everywhere, and the surface condition σ·n = t holds because nothing grips or supports the surface (t = 0). For a linear elastic body this is the only solution (Kirchhoff's uniqueness theorem: standard, not fetched). It also removes the stress of the body's own weight: held this way a car does not sag, as in orbit. What stays: self-balancing locked-in stresses (tyre pressure, bolt preload); loose contents not covered by the push; every surface force once it acts (air on the front, the ground at landing, a normal grip). A push exactly uniform per kilogram is canon, not real physics. Verifier: derivation sound.

facts.notes: Quotes: 'tidal effects arise from spatial variations of the gravitational field rather than from the field itself'; in a uniform field 'neighboring freely falling particles experience no relative acceleration, and therefore no tidal effects are present'. Eq. 1: a_x = −xGM/R³, a_y = −yGM/R³, a_z = +2zGM/R³. This is the equivalence-principle half of the gentle-hold argument: a uniform push (or field) cannot stress a body; only its gradient can. RBEF is a peer-reviewed physics-teaching journal (received 18 Mar, accepted 7 Jun 2026). Read through WebFetch; the verifier re-fetched and confirmed the quote and signs.

facts.label: Tidal stretch on a 4 m car: Earth's tide versus his spread push
facts.display: Earth's tide: about 2 mN through the middle of a 1,340 kg, 4 m car standing on end (1 part in 6 million of its weight). His push spread through it at 10 g: zero

sources.title: Benedetto (2026), Tidal forces and centrifugal gradients: a pedagogical clarification on the role of free fall and curvature, Revista Brasileira de Ensino de Física 48, doi:10.1590/1806-9126-RBEF-2026-0148
IAU 2015 Resolution B3, nominal GM of Earth (existing key earth_gm)
NASA NSSDCA Earth Fact Sheet, mean radius 6,371 km and mass (existing keys collide_earth_inertia_rotation, earth_mass)
Kelley Blue Book, 2026 Toyota Corolla specs, LE curb weight 2,955 lb (existing key toyota_corolla_curb_mass, since sourced to toyota.com’s own spec table: the same 2,955 lb)

facts.notes: Inputs: GM = 3.986004e14 m³/s² (earth_gm), R = 6.371e6 m, m = 1,340.4 kg (toyota_corolla_curb_mass), L = 4 m. Gradient 2GM/R³ = 3.08e-6 s⁻²; end to end the tidal difference is 1.2e-5 m/s² (1.3e-6 g). For a uniform rod along the vertical, mid-length tension = m L GM/(4R³) = 2.1e-3 N against a weight of 13,145 N (1 part in 6.4 million). His push, spread in proportion to mass, gives every kilogram the same acceleration, so its gradient and the stress it adds are zero at any acceleration. For contrast, 10 g through a grip puts m × 10 g = 131 kN through his hands. The 4 m is a round figure; the Corolla is 4.63 m (2.4 mN). Verifier recomputed every number.

facts.label: Spreading the force over the whole body is what raises tolerance (Eiband 1959)
facts.display: 'Survival of impact forces increases with increased distribution of the arresting force to the entire skeleton'; people cannot move against more than 2–3 g

sources.title: Eiband (1959), Human Tolerance to Rapidly Applied Accelerations: A Summary of the Literature, NASA Memorandum 5-19-59E (NTRS 19980228043)

facts.notes: Conclusions: 'complete torso and extremity support is the primary variable in increasing survival of rapidly applied accelerations. Therefore, survival of impact forces increases with increased distribution of the arresting force to the entire skeleton, for blows from all directions.' Also: 'muscular effort is inadequate for resisting anything but the mildest of impacts' and 'human beings unable to move their bodies against forces exceeding 2 or 3 times normal body weight (2 or 3 G's).' Use: a perfectly spread push is the limiting case of gentle hold and safe passenger. By the same logic a person held only by the hands, with no seat or harness, is worse off than the harnessed volunteers behind every tolerance number; by how much is not measured. Verifier re-fetched; quotes match.

facts.label: Losing consciousness from g (G-LOC) took at least 5 s in 888 centrifuge episodes
facts.display: G-LOC did not occur earlier than 5 s; mean 9.1 s for onset ≥1 G/s; levels at G-LOC ranged +2.5 to +11.7 Gz (+4.7 Gz is the curve's defined minimum)

sources.title: Whinnery & Forster (2013), The +Gz-induced loss of consciousness curve, Extreme Physiology & Medicine 2:19, doi:10.1186/2046-7648-2-19 (full text via Europe PMC)

facts.notes: Abstract: 'for onset rates ≥ 1.0 G/s, G-LOC will occur in a mean time of 9.10 s and is independent of the onset rate'; 'The minimum +Gz-level threshold tolerance was defined as +4.7 Gz'; 'G-LOC did not occur earlier than 5 s for any acceleration exposure.' +4.7 Gz is defined as 2 SD below the gradual-onset group's mean (+7.31 Gz); across all 888 episodes the +Gz level at G-LOC ranged from +2.5 to +11.7. The episodes were 'mostly in experienced military fighter pilots', with relaxed, straining and anti-G-suited runs mixed together. Use: under 5 s, loss of consciousness is unlikely (none seen in 888 episodes), but vision may still dim (Fraser: from 3–4 s); for short events, force injury is the limit. Verifier: relabelled from 'blacking out' (G-LOC is loss of consciousness, not of vision); +4.7 Gz is a curve parameter, not the lowest level seen.

facts.label: The g a passenger feels: the push from what holds them, net of gravity
facts.display: n = |a − g| / g (vectors). Standing still: 1 g. Lifted at 1 g: 2 g. Thrown (ballistic): 0 g plus drag. Under his spread push: 0 g

sources.title: ASTM F2291-06a Standard Practice for Design of Amusement Rides and Devices, as incorporated by reference (Indiana 685 IAC 1-2-9) and posted by Public.Resource.Org
NASA EG-1997-08-110-HQ, Microgravity: A Teacher's Guide with Activities in Science, Mathematics, and Technology (Rogers, Vogt & Wargo 1997), PDF pp. 14 and 17

facts.notes: Felt acceleration = (sum of contact forces)/m = a − g, with g pointing down (ASTM §7.1.4.5: limits are 'total net acceleration, inclusive of earth's gravity'). A horizontal push of a gives n = √(a² + g²)/g, so a felt 2, 4 or 6 g needs a horizontal acceleration of 1.73, 3.87 or 5.92 g. A vertical launch at a gives n = a/g + 1. Air drag in flight acts on the front, so it is felt: n_drag = ½ρv²C_dA/(m g) (comic_passenger_drag_g). value_si is the 1 g felt when standing still. Verifier: formula right; but ASTM limits are per body axis, with a combined-axis ellipse (§7.1.5.1), so compare each axis's component with that axis's curve; comparing the magnitude n with one curve is only an approximation.

facts.label: Recommended 'no harm' limit for a passenger, by body axis (safe passenger switch off)
facts.display: Orientation unknown (tumbling, a face-first catch, a push on the chest): eyes-front (−Gx) limit, 2 g at 0.2 s, 1.5 g from 0.5 s. Back-first cradle with head support (+Gx), or pushed up from below while seated upright (+Gz): 6 g to 1 s, 4 g at 2–4 s, 3 g at 5–11.8 s, then 2.5 g (+Gx) or 2 g (+Gz). Sideways 3 g → 2 g. Head-down (−Gz): as eyes-front to 4 s, then 1.1 g from 7 s. Pulses under 0.2 s: use the 0.2 s value

sources.title: ASTM F2291-06a Standard Practice for Design of Amusement Rides and Devices, as incorporated by reference (Indiana 685 IAC 1-2-9) and posted by Public.Resource.Org
Eiband (1959), Human Tolerance to Rapidly Applied Accelerations: A Summary of the Literature, NASA Memorandum 5-19-59E (NTRS 19980228043)

facts.notes: Recommendation built from verified sources. ASTM F2291 is the only published design limit for the general public (healthy riders 48 in or taller, no training), and it sits inside the layperson centrifuge results and NASA crew limits. Choices, each an estimate: (1) unknown orientation defaults to −Gx, the lowest curve over the length of a throw or catch; use 6 g only with a stated back-first cradle and head support. (2) ASTM does not cover pulses under 200 ms; each curve keeps its 0.2 s value there (Eiband: tolerance rises for shorter pulses). (3) ASTM assumes a designed seat, restraint and headrest; Rex's arms are not a seat, so treat every curve as a best case. (4) Compare per axis. (5) Children under 48 in are not covered. Carry the headrest and onset conditions (comic_passenger_onset_rate_limits). Verifier: made axis-dependent; was 6 g for every phase.

facts.display: J = Δp; F_ave = Δp / Δt

facts.label: Soft landing: the momentum the ground must still take, and the least peak force his legs allow
facts.display: Ground impulse J = m v. Time-mean ground force over a stop of T: J/T + W. Within a knee bend d, the peak force is at least m v²/(2d) + W. At 10 ft, a 0.76 m knee bend from 20 m/s needs a peak of at least 820 kN (28 × his weight)

sources.title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, §9.2 Impulse and Collisions
Nilsson & Thorstensson (1989), Ground reaction forces at different speeds of human walking and running (existing key walking_running_peak_vertical_force)

facts.notes: J = m v (add any caught object's m v). The time-mean force over a stop of T is J/T + W. Work–energy: the distance-average ground force over a stop within travel d is m v²/(2d) + W, so the PEAK force is at least that, whatever the profile. 'T ≤ 2d/v' holds only for a constant force; a long-tailed profile can have a lower time-mean but a higher peak. Absorbing the energy (½mv² + m g d) removes crater and quake, not this. d = engine strokes.leg = 0.5 × H/2 = 0.76 m at 10 ft. On two paw soles (0.62 m², engine estimate) that is 1.3 MPa at 20 m/s; on Ollie's boot soles (0.30 m²), 2.7 MPa. Above the ground's bearing capacity he still sinks unless comic ground is on. Holding it to the walking load (1.2 W) needs T = v/(0.2 g): 2.5 s from 5 m/s, impossible on his feet. Earth's recoil energy J²/(2M_E) is 2e-17 to 8e-15 J. Verifier: peak-force rule stated; impossible cells flagged.

facts.label: Momentum cannot be passed on with zero energy: at least p²/(2M) stays in whatever takes it
facts.display: Passing momentum p to a body of mass M leaves at least p²/(2M) in that body. For the Earth this is effectively nothing; for a small mass of air it can be large, though it shrinks as the moving air spreads

sources.title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, §9.2 Impulse and Collisions

facts.notes: A body of mass M at rest given momentum p moves at p/M and carries kinetic energy p²/(2M) (its centre-of-mass energy), the least any receiver can end up with, so an absorbed switch can absorb everything except this. Example: a 3,007 kg Rex landing at 100 m/s passes p = 3.0e5 N s to the Earth (5.97e24 kg), which keeps 7.6e-15 J. That is why soft landing can absorb the energy and still pass on the momentum. Cool flight: at any moment the air carrying the momentum holds at least p²/(2 m_air); that bound shrinks as the wake spreads and more air shares the momentum, and the bulk motion ends as heat. Silent strike: the fist's own momentum returns through his arm and feet to the Earth; the small drag impulse the fist gives the air still goes to the air. Verifier: 'impossible' for cool flight was overstated; reworded.

facts.display: About 5 × 10²³ J, estimated from the 80–100 km transient crater; the abstract rounds this to "about 10²³ joules"

facts.notes: Main text: "the apparent diameter of the transient crater ... is estimated to be between 80 km and 100 km ... and the impact energy is estimated to be about 5 × 10^23 J"; "For an asteroid speed of around 18 km s–1 and impact angles of between 45° and 60°, impactor diameters of around 12.2–14.4 km are required". facts.label: Sound from a body whose volume changes (acoustic monopole)
facts.display: p(r, t) = ρ₀ V̈(t − r/c₀) / (4πr), from R&H eq. 2.61: the pressure is set by the second time-derivative of the body's volume; steady expansion makes no sound in this approximation

sources.title: Rienstra & Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics (Eindhoven University of Technology lecture text, PDF version dated 6 Sep 2026)

facts.notes: R&H p. 24, eq. (2.61): "mass injection is a source of sound, primarily because of the displacement of a volume fraction β of the original fluid". Section 6.2, p. 150 (pulsating sphere): "If (∂a/∂t)/c0 ≪ 1, we can use linear acoustics"; for a compact sphere "the second derivative to time of the volume of the sphere is the source of sound. A steady expansion of the sphere (∂a/∂t = constant) does not (in this approximation) generate sound." For large radii the wall acts as "a piston which generates plane waves." Curle's theorem (6.85, p. 170) extends this to any compact pulsating body. The explicit 4πr form is our standard step with the free-field Green's function (6.37). Valid when c0 × growth time ≫ body size and surface speed ≪ c0. Verifier: quotes confirmed; formula labelled 'from eq. 2.61'; a line-source check shows r = R_eq + d is mildly conservative for his tall shape.
facts.who_when: Rienstra & Hirschberg (TU Eindhoven), after Lighthill and Curle

facts.label: A volume source on the ground: pressure doubled
facts.display: Next to a rigid wall or ground a monopole's pressure is 2 times its free-field value: p = ρ₀ V̈ / (2πr)

sources.title: Rienstra & Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics (Eindhoven University of Technology lecture text, PDF version dated 6 Sep 2026)

facts.notes: Rienstra & Hirschberg, exercises to chapter 6, p. 172 (PDF p. 181), item f: "The acoustic pressure p′ generated by a monopole close to a wall increases by a factor 2 in comparison with free field conditions." Applied to Rex standing on the ground. Real ground is not perfectly rigid, so 2 is the conservative (upper) factor. Verifier: quote confirmed.

facts.label: Gradual growth: peak air pressure at a bystander, and the shortest duration that keeps it harmless
facts.display: p_peak = ρ₀ k_V ΔV / (2π r T²); for pure size with a smooth start and stop, p_peak = ρ₀ ΔV / (r T²), so T_min = √(ρ₀ ΔV / (r p_safe))

sources.title: Rienstra & Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics (Eindhoven University of Technology lecture text, PDF version dated 6 Sep 2026)

facts.notes: Inputs: monopole on rigid ground, p = ρ0 V̈/(2πr) (growth_monopole_compact_body, growth_monopole_ground_doubling); ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³ (atm_isa_sea_level_density). Profile (our choice): fraction of mass added s(t) = t/T − sin(2πt/T)/(2π), so the rate ∝ 1 − cos(2πt/T) starts and ends at zero. Pure size: k_V = max|V̈|·T²/ΔV = 2π exactly. Mix grows fastest early: k_V = 14.3 (k = 371), 17.9 (1,555), 54.7 (1.4e6). Pure density: no pulse. r = R_eq(final) + d. Valid while c0·T ≫ his height and surface speed ≪ 340 m/s. Longer than 0.05 s, the pulse is infrasound: felt, not heard. Ignores terrain and buildings. Verifier: k_V reproduced. The wind term is not always negligible: at the 100 Pa duration, displaced air blows about 3 m/s (½ρu² ≈ 6 Pa) for Chicxulub pure size and 5.4 m/s (18 Pa) for one solar second pure size; negligible at the longer shove-limited durations.

facts.display: Safe limit for houses: 134 dB on a 0.1 Hz high-pass meter (0.0145 psi, 100 Pa). Rattling complaints begin above about 120 dB on a 6 Hz meter (about 36 Pa unfiltered by our conversion: see the row "Rattling onset as an unfiltered peak pressure"); some homes still rattle below the safe limit

sources.title: Siskind, Stachura, Stagg & Kopp (1980) Structure Response and Damage Produced by Airblast from Surface Mining, US Bureau of Mines Report of Investigations 8485 (copy hosted by the Resolution Copper Mine EIS)

facts.notes: Abstract: "Safe levels of airblast were found to be 134 dBL (0.1 Hz), 133 dBL (2Hz), 129 dBL (6Hz), and 105 dB C-slow." Rattling "will not entirely be precluded by the recommended levels". p. 66: "Levels exceeding 120 dB will produce some annoyance from rattling and fright, with as much as 5 to 10 pct of homes exhibiting such disturbances at the maximum level of 134 dBL (0.1-Hz high-pass)." Text: "complaints about rattling occur at airblast levels exceeding about 120 dB (6Hz)". Table 13 (annoyance) lists 0.0145 psi beside 134 dBL. p = 20 µPa × 10^(L/20): 134 dB = 100 Pa. As 129 dB (6 Hz) matches 134 dBL (0.1 Hz), 120 dB (6 Hz) is about 125 dB unfiltered, 36 Pa (our conversion). The 2 s limit is stated for C-slow only.
