facts.notes: NASA page: "p1 / p0 = [2* gam * M^2 - (gam - 1)] / (gam + 1)" and "r1 / r0 = [(gam + 1) * M^2 ] / [(gam -1 ) * M^2 + 2]" (M = upstream Mach number in the shock frame). γ = 1.4 (existing atm_ratio_specific_heats_air). Verifier: equations confirmed verbatim.

facts.label: Air pressure in front of a flat surface pushed suddenly at speed u (piston shock)
facts.display: Δp = p₀·(2γ/(γ+1))·(M² − 1), M = (γ+1)u/(4c₀) + √[((γ+1)u/(4c₀))² + 1]. Slow: Δp ≈ ρ₀c₀u. Fast: Δp ≈ 1.2 ρ₀u². At 405 m/s: 330 kPa

sources.title: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics: Normal Shock Wave
Collins, Melosh & Marcus (2005) Earth Impact Effects Program, Eq. 59* (existing key blast_collins_peak_wind_speed): the same relation written for γ = 1.4

facts.notes: From the normal-shock relations: gas behind a shock moving at M·c0 into still air moves at u = (2c0/(γ+1))(M − 1/M); invert for M and use the pressure jump. Weak limit (u ≪ c0): Δp → ρ0 c0 u (the acoustic piston). Strong limit: Δp → ((γ+1)/2) ρ0 u² = 1.2 ρ0 u². For γ = 1.4 this is algebraically identical to the existing verified Collins/Glasstone wind relation u = (5p/7P0)c0/√(1 + 6p/7P0). Table (ISA air): u = 10 m/s gives 4.2 kPa; 100 gives 50 kPa; 340 gives 250 kPa; 405 gives 330 kPa; 1,000 gives 1.58 MPa; 1,540 gives 3.6 MPa. Use: the pressure on a large body's surface just after it suddenly starts moving (R&H: a large, fast sphere acts as a plane piston), and an upper bound afterwards, since a sphere lets air escape sideways. Verifier: inversion, table and the Collins identity reproduced; dropped a reference to a 'strong-shock form' that the brief does not contain.

facts.label: Taylor's expanding sphere (1946), as described by Courant & Friedrichs
facts.display: A sphere expanding at constant speed drives a constant-speed shock; the air behind it keeps compressing up to the surface; the shock is much weaker than a flat piston's at the same speed

sources.title: Courant & Friedrichs (1948) Supersonic Flow and Shock Waves, Interscience; scan at the Internet Archive (dli.ernet.177550), sections 158 and 162, pp. 416-428, Fig. 12
Courant & Friedrichs (1948), Internet Archive OCR text of the same scan (the quotes were read here; the scan PDF has no text layer)
Taylor, G. I. (1946) The air wave surrounding an expanding sphere, Proc. R. Soc. A 186:273-292 (bibliographic record only; full text not readable)

facts.notes: C&F p. 417: "an energy supply at an increasing rate is required to maintain constant speed of the piston." Section 162, p. 427: "the shock speed Ξ can be determined as function of the prescribed velocity ξ0 of the surface of the sphere. The solution of the problem, first worked out by G. I. Taylor, is thus established"; the gas "suffers a further compression" behind the shock. p. 428: Taylor found sound theory gave "too high a value" for the pressure near the sphere at 0.2c0. Fig. 12 plots sphere and gas speed against shock speed Ξ: ξ0 = c0 at Ξ ≈ 1.3 c0, 2c0 at Ξ ≈ 2.2 c0. Taylor's paper and tables were not readable. Verifier: quotes confirmed in the OCR text (source added); Crossref confirms Taylor 1946. Digitising Fig. 12: printed ξ0 reads 0.04–0.06 c0 above an exact solution, the gas-speed curve 0.01–0.02 above exact Rankine–Hugoniot, so the real gap is about 0.03–0.04 c0.

facts.label: Surface pressure on a sphere expanding at constant speed (our solution of Taylor's problem)
facts.display: Δp at the surface ≈ ρ₀u², within 2% from 0.8 to 9 times the speed of sound; 1.15 ρ₀u² at 0.3 c₀, rising toward 1.5 ρ₀u² for slow growth. At u = c₀: 1.4 atm, against 2.5 atm for a flat piston. Holds only when his final size is much larger than his starting size

facts.notes: Self-similar isentropic flow behind a constant-speed shock, integrated from the Rankine–Hugoniot state in to the sphere surface. Checked with a 1-D spherical Lagrangian hydro code: u = c0 gives shock 1.328 c0 and Δp 1.41 p0 (similarity 1.329, 1.417); 2c0 gives 2.263 c0, 5.60 p0 (2.264, 5.66). Δp/(ρ0u²): 1.08 (0.45 c0), 1.04 (0.6), 1.02 (0.8), 1.01 (1.0), 1.00 (1.5 and above); 1.15–1.16 at 0.3 c0 (hydro code). Our sphere-speed curve lies 0.04–0.05 c0 below the printed Fig. 12. The shock-fitted solution cannot go below about 0.31 c0; as u → 0 the factor tends to the incompressible 1.5 (verifier's derivation, not sourced). The solution starts from zero size, so it applies only when R_final ≫ R0 (growth much longer than R0/c0 = 2.6 ms); otherwise use the flat-piston onset ρ0c0u (growth_piston_shock_planar). facts.label: Gravitational binding energy of a uniform ball (Newtonian and general-relativistic)
facts.display: Newtonian: 3GM²/(5R). Exact for a uniform ball in general relativity: BE/M = (3/4β)[sin⁻¹√(2β)/√(2β) − √(1 − 2β)] − 1 ≈ 3β/5 + 9β²/14 + …, with β = GM/(Rc²)

sources.title: Lattimer & Prakash (2001) Neutron Star Structure and the Equation of State, ApJ 550:426; arXiv:astro-ph/0002232, section 6, eqs. (33)-(35)

facts.notes: Lattimer & Prakash section 6: "The binding energy formally represents the energy gained by assembling N baryons ... BE = N m_b − M in mass units." "In the cases of the incompressible fluid and the Buchdahl solution, analytic results for the binding energy can be found", eq. (34): BE_Inc/M = (3/4β)[sin⁻¹√(2β)/√(2β) − √(1 − 2β)] − 1 ≈ 3β/5 + 9β²/14 + 5β³/6 + ···, with β ≡ GM/Rc². The leading term 3β/5 × Mc² is the Newtonian 3GM²/(5R); the series at β = 0.01 gives 0.0060651. A primary citation for the 3/5 formula that energy_earth_gravitational_binding takes from Wikipedia. For Rex at canon: 3GM²/(5R) = 4.1e-4 J; β = 2.5e-24. Verifier: eq. (34) confirmed, and independently checked that it equals the proper-mass integral for uniform density, so the M_p = M(1 + g) use is correct.

facts.label: Can the growth loop run away outside a black hole?
facts.display: No. Shoving the air returns about 10⁻¹⁵ of the energy (less for mix, none for pure density); pushing rock aside at most about 4 × 10⁻¹¹; any ordinary matter at most a few × 10⁻⁸. Their own gravity returns a share that reaches 1 only at the event horizon, so the half-life only matters once he is already a black hole. This covers energy feedback only, not the momentum of instant growth. Under the canon (owner and collaborator, 12 Oct 2026) the energy gravity releases goes to the endless ocean, so the loop never runs away and the page has no half-life control.

gaps.step:
Not found or not verified, from the researcher's gaps and the verifier's missing list. None of the items below was fetched and confirmed, so none is a fact here.
- Standard footfall force model used in vibration engineering: the Fourier-series walking load, with a first-harmonic dynamic load factor of about 0.4–0.5 body weight at the step rate, smaller higher harmonics, and an effective heel-impact impulse for stiff structures (ISO 10137, AISC Design Guide 11, SCI P354, CCIP-016; the Živanović et al. 2005 J Sound Vib review is an open candidate). The verifier names this as the biggest gap: without it the step is not in the form vibration methods actually use.
- Frequency content of a footstep force: step rate about 1.1–1.8 Hz for Rex and Ollie, and heel-impact content up to about 1/(time to peak), tens of Hz. No measured seismic or vibration signature of human footsteps was fetched (e.g. Ekimov & Sabatier, JASA). The brief needs one as a human anchor for 'footsteps you can feel'.
- Compliant ground: every force and loading rate here was measured on rigid force plates. Walking on sand (Lejeune et al. 1998, JEB, 1.6–2.5× energy cost) and any measured force or loading rate on sand or turf were not fetched. On soft ground the peaks and rates would be lower, by an unknown amount.
- Walking heel-strike transient size in body weights: Whittle 1999 and Verdini 2006 full texts are paywalled. Describe the impact by heel speed and energy (Baines 2018), not as a force spike in body weights.
- Directly measured human stance time at preferred speed: Öberg 1993 failed TLS on the VA site, and Bohannon's per-decade table is paywalled. Stance is computed as duty factor × stride period; label it 'computed'.
- Drill stamp: foot speed, contact duration and individual (not group-mean) maximum forces are not reported. Stamp speed, effective mass and energy are estimates; the measured forces (group means 3.1–6.6 BW) are what the page can show as measured.
- Footprints: only one anchor (one weighed elephant, one sand). A measured human footprint depth in dry or loose sand (D'Août et al. 2010; Bennett or Morse experiments) and Platt et al. 2012 (elephant track volumes versus moisture) were not read. Footprint depths in loose dry sand, wet sand and mud remain unanchored: say 'estimate, no measured anchor'. The engine's loose-sand failure rule (a person sinking about 0.2 m per step) could not be tested against a measured human print.
- Langman et al. 1995 (elephant minimum cost of transport at 1.0 m/s in three mid-sized African elephants), known only as cited in Hutchinson 2006 per the verifier. The primary was not read. It would be a better basis for a 'comfortable elephant pace' than the unsupported 'Froude about 0.1 self-selected'.
- Elephant hip heights behind Panagiotopoulou's Froude numbers (1.2 m/s at 0.07 implies about 2.1 m) and limb forces for adult (not juvenile) elephants.
- Boot attenuation for Ollie is not quantified. Rawcliffe 2020 reports significant differences between three kinds of footwear, but the abstract gives no numbers; the full text was not read. Lafortune & Hennig 1992 give no usable number.
- Alexander 1989 (Physiol Rev) and Alexander & Jayes 1983 (J Zool) were not read; Alexander 2004 (J Anat) and Kram 1997 were used instead.
- Hutchinson 2006 tables were read through WebFetch because the PDF sat behind a Cloudflare challenge; its regression log base is not stated.
- Ren 2010 walking peaks per limb (0.55 and 0.36 BW) were read off a small figure (±0.03). Ren's subjects were juveniles of about 2.3 t.
- Panagiotopoulou 2016: the text's 946 kPa 'mean peak' against the table's 224–318 kPa per foot is unresolved; use the table. Its elephant masses are keepers' estimates.
- Schanz 2013 does not print the measured foot speed (back-calculated at about 1.0 m/s). Its dynamic factor implies a 1.1 BW forefoot peak, double the force-plate value: mark it disputed if shown.
- EM 1110-1-1904 (USACE settlement manual) could not be fetched; FHWA GEC 5 was used instead, and its Eq. 8.16 is an image, so the formula's form is inferred from its stated variables.
- Rex's and Ollie's hip height (0.45 H) is our measurement from the turnarounds, an estimate until the turnarounds are remeasured. Heel-first walking is canon (owners, 12 Oct 2026).
- Decker 2003's 3.4 BW for a 60 cm drop landing is known only as cited by Carden 2015 (reported).
- Not in this topic: the sound of steps, seismic attenuation and the elephant seismic measurements (O'Connell-Rodwell, Mortimer), and perception and damage thresholds.
gaps.attenuation:
Not found or not verified (the researcher's gaps and the verifier's missing list). None of these was fetched and confirmed, so none is a fact here.
- Walking regime unchecked: no measured ground PPV against distance for footsteps (people, animals, horses) or for slow quasi-static loads (for example Auersch's train data). The ramp and near-field branch, the Walk tab's main case, has no measured check. A search snippet that footsteps 'did not exceed 3 × 10⁻⁶ m/s at 3 m' could not be traced to its source and is not used.
- Long range: no low-energy (about 1–100 kJ) impact data beyond 60 m, which is needed to choose between the model's steep damped fall-off (r^-2 to r^-3 for stamps on soft ground) and the measured r^-1.0 to r^-1.6. Model results beyond 60 m are untested and probably too low for stamps (verifier: by roughly 3–10× at 200 m if the measured exponents hold).
- Low-energy drops: one site in range (Pisa, 3.8 kJ), plus 82 kJ (TRL Fig. 44) and the 1–12 MJ compaction data. Nothing measured at 10 J–1 kJ on soil.
- The 10 J–10 kJ 'footstep energy' range used in the extrapolation argument has no stated physical basis.
- Small-strain thresholds and damping: no source for the 10⁻⁴ strain flag or for damping ratios by soil type (candidates: Vucetic 1994; Darendeli 2001; Seed & Idriss).
- Building amplification: Lauzon's 2–4 is unsourced; USBM RI 8507 (Siskind et al. 1980), a public report and the likely origin, was not fetched.
- Near-surface shear-wave speeds for the specific surfaces (SASW or MASW profiles of loose sand, road subgrade, soft clay crusts) and the effect of layering or a water table at 1–2 m on surface waves: not researched. The surface values are picks inside 30 m class ranges.
- Primary sources not fetched: Pekeris 1955 and Kausel 2012 (closed form rebuilt and checked numerically), Miller & Pursey 1955 (numbers via Sánchez-Sesma et al. 2011), Mayne et al. 1984 and Mayne 1985 (data ranges unknown), Woods & Jedele 1985, Amick 1999/2000, Gutowski & Dym 1976, Kim & Lee 2000. There is no verified table of soil damping α at a stated frequency.
- Elephant stomps: amplitudes are secondary (arXiv 2024); the elephants' masses and stomp forces were not seen. The elephant topic should fetch O'Connell-Rodwell et al. 2000 in full.
- Lake ice (flexural-gravity waves) and steel deck (plate resonance): not researched; the page should say ground shaking is not modelled on them. The steel shear speed (3.2 km/s) is an unsourced estimate.
- Step-force inputs (footstep rise times, heel-strike transients, stamp contact times) belong to the step-force topic; the examples here use placeholders. The two-foot cancellation in walking (up to 2× lower far away) is unquantified.
gaps.elephant: (1) O'Connell-Rodwell, Arnason & Hart (2000) JASA 108:3066-72 was not read (paywalled; publisher and ResearchGate 403; OpenAlex/Unpaywall closed). The stomp values (48.7 and 17.0 µm/s peak-to-peak at 3–12 m and 40 m), the rumble values (0.437 and 0.264 µm/s RMS) and the 24.03 Hz stomp frequency come from a secondary quote (Wijayaraja et al. 2024), so they and the halved zero-to-peak values are 'reported'. Unknown: the exact distances inside '3–12 m', the ground, the elephants' masses, and whether the stomps were mock-charge stomps (our inference from the matching 32 km in the authors' SICB abstract). On the page say 'reported by a later paper', not 'measured'. (2) Full text not read: Szenicer et al. 2022 (publisher bot check; abstract via Crossref), Günther et al. 2004 (rumbles only), O'Connell-Rodwell 2001 and 2007 (abstracts without numbers). Reinwald et al. 2021 was read but gives no footfall amplitudes. (3) Steinmann et al. 2025: every amplitude is a pixel reading of a printed figure converted with one dominant frequency (expect ±30–50%); each panel is one 10 s record of one animal at a camera-trap distance; the paper does not describe instrument correction (a Guralp 6TD is reported only by a secondary source). The horizontal components were recorded but not digitized. The authors' Methods Blog says giraffe steps shake the ground 'in the order of tens of micrometers', which conflicts with the paper's figures (about 0.1 µm at most); the blog was not used. (4) Mortimer et al. 2018: the Fig. 1D fast-walk distance is not given (only '2 to 30 m'); the calibration wording ('multiplying by ... 23.4 V m-1 s-1') is unclear, and the half-space check is consistent with it only within a factor of a few if the elephant was within 2–5 m, so it does not confirm it. The terrain noise distributions in Fig. S1B were not digitized. (5) Masses: none of the field seismic studies weighed wild elephants; only Wijayaraja et al. 2024 (2,700–3,500 kg, captive, E3 ridden by a mahout) and the non-seismic Ren & Hutchinson 2008 (2,550–3,230 kg, aged 12–14) did. The step topic's step_elephant_body_mass_larramendi2016 and step_elephant_match_3007kg give the adult averages; the brief's 'about as much as an African elephant' should read 'about as heavy as a female African elephant'. (6) Other animals: no absolute ground-velocity measurements of horses or cattle were found; Wood 2005's giraffe, gemsbok, kudu, lion and human records are normalized. Human footstep geophone work (Ekimov & Sabatier 2006/2011, Pakhomov et al. 2003, ARL/DTIC reports) was seen only as abstracts; no human amplitude other than Steinmann's single human at 53 m (mass and gait unknown) is included. (7) Synthesis: no study gives footfall amplitude against distance for one elephant at one site with calibrated sensors. The 1/D law (5–100 m), n = 1 and the ×0.15–×8 band are our estimate. (8) Verifier's missing items not added as facts: a check of the 'few percent of body weight in the seismic band' claim against measured elephant ground reaction forces and stance times (Ren & Hutchinson 2008 GRF data not used; the step topic's step_ren2010_elephant_limb_forces gives a forefoot peak of about 0.55 body weights, not combined here); horizontal-component amplitudes and real H/V on soft ground; a sourced Q or α for sandy soils near 20 Hz (the only fitted α is for 40–60 Hz on calcrete). (9) Cautions for the model, from the verifier's review of the recommendation: do not carry α = 0.02–0.05 per m (fitted at 40–60 Hz) to 20 Hz without scaling (at constant Q about 0.008–0.022 per m), and do not combine an e^(−αr) model with the separate 1/D anchor as two decay laws; the half-space formula is the Rayleigh-pole far field only and is invalid within about one wavelength (6 m at Vs 120, 12.5 m at Vs 250, 30 m at Vs 600 at 20 Hz), so it needs a near-field term or a stated minimum distance; Mayne's compaction-drop law (PPV = 70(√(WH)/d)^1.4) would be used at scaled distances of about 0.001–0.03, below the typical fitted range (not verified here), so label any use for footsteps as an extrapolation; there is no general 'below noise beyond 100–150 m' rule (Steinmann's 150 m is a dataset cut-off, Wijayaraja's 155.6 m was space-limited, Mortimer models 0.4–3.6 km; only Wood's ~100 m at Etosha is a measured detection radius); drop the '1.2× vector peak' bound (true vector peak equals the vertical for an ideal Rayleigh wave); ground multipliers should depend on distance (the half-space sand-to-rock ratio is ×72 at 20 m and should shrink with distance because loose sand damps more); the band is about 50-fold wide, so 'about like an elephant' must show that width; Mortimer's 0.21–0.36 mm/s sits outside the band at every D ≥ 5 m and is reconciled only by an unverified 'within about 2 m'; the elephant's cushioned feet are not the authors' explanation of its weak amplitude. (10) Working files: the researcher's downloads and scripts (digitize.py, scal.py, derive.py, lamb.py) are in scratchpad/research/elephant/; the verifier's (dig2.py, dig3.py, scal.py, lamb_check.py, derive_check.py) in scratchpad/research/elephant-check/.
gaps.thresholds:
What is still missing or unverified, and what the page should do about it:
- Footstep frequency and duration: the dominant frequency and length of a step's ground vibration are not part of this topic, and the engine's ppvAt has no frequency. The rattle option, the BS 7385-2 curve, the 1 g marker and the footing option all swing with f (rattle 4.4 mm/s at 5 Hz against 1.1 at 20 Hz; 1 g at 312 against 78 mm/s). Until the attenuation research gives f, show frequency-dependent values at a stated assumed frequency and call it an assumption. Caltrans assumes 10-30 Hz for construction and traffic. The verifier thinks the engine's law (k = 0.070 m/s, n = 1.4, E0 = 1 t m) looks like a heavy-tamper dynamic-compaction law, which may be low in frequency; not verified.
- Rattling: no standard, agency guide or measurement gives a ground PPV at which windows or crockery rattle. Caltrans, its TA, FTA and USBM say only that rattling happens at or below perception. The 1 mm/s default comes from earthquake intensity IV acceleration converted at an assumed 20 Hz; it is an estimate and sits above the sources' own statements.
- Losing footing: nothing covers loss of footing under vertical or short impulsive ground motion. The 300 mm/s value rests on horizontal earthquake shaking (EMS-98 wording on Wald 1999 PGV bands) and one small shake-table study whose onset is set by its test grid (Takahashi 2004: 30 young subjects, horizontal sinusoids, 'have not find clear limit value'). Whether footsteps make people lose footing sooner or later is unknown; 1 g vertical, g/(2 pi f), is a physics marker for lift-off.
- Components: Wald/ShakeMap values are the larger horizontal component, Whiffin & Leonard's are vertical, BS 5228-2/7385-2 use the peak component. Which component ppvAt predicts is unstated.
- Paywalled standards not opened: BS 7385-2 (seen via BS 5228-2 and An Bord Pleanala), DIN 4150-3 (1999 via Watercare; 2016 via An Bord Pleanala, whose dwellings 50-100 Hz cell '40 to 50' conflicts with 1999's '15 to 20', so disputed), ISO 2631 (via Caltrans, which dates its guide 1981, and Watercare, which cites the 1989 edition; the 2003 edition's lack of limits is a consultant's statement), BS 6472-1 (only HS2's VDV criteria). The BS 5228-2 A1:2014 footnotes and the Irish EPA guidance were seen only in An Bord Pleanala's reproduction.
- Wald 1999 itself is paywalled; the USGS manual's reproduction was used. Below intensity V its PGV relation was imposed, not fitted; some printed PGA edges above V do not follow the manual's equation. ShakeMap now uses Worden et al. (2012), not fetched.
- Siskind's damage probabilities come from two reproductions (Caltrans, Watercare) that disagree on the last column's heading (90% against 100%); neither was checked against RI 8507's probability plots (figs. 55-59).
- Seen only as reproduced: Whiffin & Leonard (LR 418), Wiss (1974), Wiss & Parmelee (1974), Reiher & Meister (1931), Atherton, Murray, Stagg et al., Chae, Konan, Dowding, AASHTO and the Swiss standard. The FTA manual's official URL returned 403; the identical ROSA P copy was used.
- Indoor response: indoor amplification is sourced only as typical USBM factors (1.5 whole house, 4 midwalls, below 1 above 40 Hz) and the RI 8507 test-house floor velocities. Human criteria are set for people indoors; FTA says ground vibration is 'almost never a problem outdoors'.
gaps.ripple: No measured naked-eye threshold for visible ripples in a glass at footstep frequencies (10-40 Hz) was found, by the researcher or by the verifier's two further searches; exact query strings were not logged. Both page thresholds (ripple_threshold_shimmer, ripple_threshold_rings) are estimates: derived, not measured. Open items, none fetched or confirmed: (1) Visibility criterion: the 10-arcmin 'noticeable' factor is a guess, ten times the sourced 1-arcmin acuity; it is the largest uncertainty (about a factor of 10). Webvision's hyperacuity chapter and motion-detection literature could tighten it. (2) Glass contact angle: water on household soda-lime glass, clean versus used, is unsourced (0-50° assumed); a PMC table with one glass value (45°) was behind a captcha. The ring threshold scales with meniscus height. (3) Ring (meniscus) radiation model: the verifier's own Green's-function derivation, checked numerically but not from a paper; no paper gives edge-wave height against forcing. (4) Capillary wavemaker theory: Hocking & Mahdmina 1991 (JFM 224) and the full text of Cocciaro, Faetti & Nobili 1991 (JFM 231) would replace the gravity-only ratio of 2. (5) Floor and table transfer: no source for amplification from ground to table top; suspended floors and tables often resonate at 10-30 Hz and could amplify several-fold. AISC Design Guide 11 and SCI P354 are candidates. (6) Component convention: shimmer responds to horizontal and rings to vertical motion; the threshold topic's PPV convention and an H/V ratio (about 0.7 for Rayleigh waves in a uniform half-space, textbook, not sourced here) need settling. (7) Pulse versus steady shaking: thresholds are for steady sinusoids; a footstep is a burst of a few cycles, which cannot build up the glass's resonant edge-wave peaks. (8) Faraday onset in an ordinary part-filled glass (moving contact line) was not measured; the Shao figures are for a brimful pinned tank and may be peak-to-peak. (9) Worden et al. (2012) was not fetched; the MMI IV band of 0.65-3.1 cm/s uses recalled coefficients. (10) Film production: no primary Lantieri interview was fetched, and the secondary sources conflict. (11) Human perception thresholds (BS 5228-2, ISO 2631-2) belong to the threshold topic and are not restated here. Fetch failures: the Clemson copy of Shao et al. 2021 JFM returned 503 (NSF PAR copy used); APS DFD abstracts returned 403; the Leicester Physics Special Topics search does not work in a plain fetch.
gaps.comic:
Not found or not verified:
- Current ASTM F2291 edition. The ASTM store lists F2291-26 (June 2026) as active and a reseller lists F2291-26a (Aug 2026); neither was checked. The limits here are F2291-06a (Public.Resource.Org copy). EN 13814:2019 was not fetched. Say 'ASTM F2291-06a (later editions may differ)'.
- Any measured tolerance for a person held or carried by hand, or for soft tissue squeezed by a grip, or for head and neck support (whiplash) without a headrest beyond ASTM's headrest rule. Every limit found assumes a seat or harness: on the page, 'for someone held in his hands, nobody has measured it; these limits are a best case'.
- Pulses under 200 ms for ordinary, unrestrained people. ASTM does not cover them; Eiband's numbers are for fully harnessed volunteers. Keeping each curve's 0.2 s value is an estimate.
- Onset rates of Rex's throw and catch strokes: not modelled; the ride limit is under 15 g/s from 0 g and 5 g/s without a headrest (comic_passenger_onset_rate_limits).
- Ground-landing injury for a thrown, uncaught passenger (injury against impact speed or fall height): no source. Any uncaught throw has an unquantified landing hazard; the fastest ride-limit launch lands at about 16 m/s, like a 13 m fall.
- How far a person's body gives on landing, so the landing g is unknown unless he catches them.
- Windblast injury thresholds for an unprotected person at 1.2–7.2 kPa dynamic pressure (44–108 m/s); only the drag g is derived.
- Children under 48 in, elderly or pregnant passengers: the ride limits do not cover them.
- Primary papers read only as reproduced or summarised: Cochran et al. 1954 (via SP-3006 Table 4-4, which gives no onset rate or posture); Fraser 1966; Perkins & Jackson, Windes, Poulter, Reed, Blume, Wiggins and Sutherland (via USBM RI 8485); Beeding & Mosely 1960 and Stapp (via SP-3006). NIOSH 1998's 140 dB limit was not fetched (OSHA's was).
- Kirchhoff's uniqueness theorem (the stress-free solution is the only one) is standard but was not fetched.
- The sonic boom from a supersonic fist or hand, and the airblast from a clap in dB with its frequency content. The engine gives only peak overpressure; rattle and damage thresholds depend on pulse length and on the measuring system (RI 8485's 120 dB and 129 dB are on a 6 Hz system, 134 dB on 0.1 Hz). Call dB thresholds approximate.
- Cool flight: the share of drag energy that heats the object rather than the air, and how fast the air's residual p²/(2 m_air) falls as the wake spreads.
- Motion sickness or discomfort from the few seconds of weightlessness that safe passenger produces: not quantified. Say 'people feel weightless, as on a drop ride; some find it unpleasant'.
Access notes: the NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D link on nasa.gov returned 404, so Rev F (approved 2026-07-14) was used from a standards.nasa.gov 'system/files/tmp' path. NCBI Bookshelf and StatPearls blocked automated fetches, so G-LOC figures come from SP-3006 and Whinnery & Forster 2013. The VDV ride-limits paper (Rohde 2024) could not be fetched (expired TLS certificate). The centrifuge studies were read as abstracts only (Europe PMC); their subjects were screened, seated and strapped in.
On the page, call the passenger limits 'the limits used for fairground rides', not 'safe for anyone'.
gaps.growth: Not read, or only partly verified: (1) Taylor (1946) itself: publisher page behind a bot check, no PubMed abstract. Its content comes from Courant & Friedrichs (OCR text and Fig. 12) plus our own similarity solution, checked with a hydro code; the printed sphere-speed curve sits about 0.03–0.05 c0 above our solution, and Taylor's tables were not seen. Page: 'Taylor's result as reproduced by Courant & Friedrichs; surface pressures from our own calculation.' (2) Kinsler et al. and Pierce not opened (Springer blocked); the monopole formula rests on Rienstra & Hirschberg eq. 2.61. (3) 250 mm/s: ANSI/RIA R15.06 and ISO 10218 are paywalled; the value comes from the OSHA Technical Manual's teach-mode description, where the person also holds a stop device. No source gives a harmless speed for a person pushed by a massive moving surface. Page: 'borrowed from robot safety; not tested for this case.' (4) 1,540 m/s in soft tissue: review-level PMC sources; IEC/ICRU originals not fetched. Canon does not say what Rex is made of inside. (5) Krakatoa's total energy: no primary source. Only Harkrider & Press's air-wave equivalent (100–150 Mt) is primary. Quoted estimates run 1e17–6.3e18 J (1–70 kg); one preprint infers up to 12 Gt (560 kg). Page: 'estimates differ a lot'. (6) Long, smooth pressure pulses: no threshold found for pulses lasting seconds. USBM's levels are for blast pulses; its 120 dB rattle onset is on a 6 Hz meter (about 36 Pa unfiltered, our conversion) and does not transfer to slow pulses. The 3.4 kPa window and 34.5 kPa eardrum presets are fast-blast thresholds, not tested for smooth pulses. (7) Energy-to-TNT equivalence for a piston-driven blast is sourced only as an upper limit beyond R̄ ≈ 2 (Baker 1977, gas-vessel bursts); nearer, the surface pressure is used. (8) Relativistic loop: uniform-density result, valid for a perfect fluid only up to β = 4/9 (Buchdahl); beyond that only because he is indestructible. The rest-mass versus gravitational-mass reading is our reasoning, not sourced. The 1 − √(1 − 2β) infall factor is standard but not separately sourced. (9) The incompressible 1.5 ρ0u² limit for slow sphere expansion is the verifier's derivation, not sourced. Raised by the verifier but not added as facts (computed, not fetched): (a) Momentum in instant growth: with soles fixed, his centre of mass rises at about half the head speed (about 700 m/s, momentum 3.3e9 kg·m/s, for Chicxulub pure size); the ground force reaches about 4.7 GPa under his grown soles (twice under Ollie's boots), and he would be thrown about 25 km up unless held down. Anchoring at the centre of mass instead drives his feet into the ground. The engine needs a momentum and lift-off check for both instant and gradual growth (lift-off T ≥ about √(πΔH/g), about 3 s for Chicxulub pure size). Folded into growth_ground_push_estimate. (b) Clear-space precondition for gradual growth: buildings, vehicles or trees inside his final footprint (equivalent radius 10 m for Chicxulub pure size, 99 m for a Sun-second) are pushed over or crushed at any speed; only people who can step away are protected. (c) Shape factors for the canon bodies (centre-of-mass height fraction; largest horizontal reach of tail, snout and arms from the soles) should be measured from the turnarounds; the 0.29 equivalent-ball side factor is an assumption. (d) Ollie inputs: 3.06 m tall and 0.15 m² boot soles (existing estimate rex_ollie_picture_build; Rex's paw 0.31 m²), so his ground stresses are about twice Rex's. (e) Black-hole threshold uses the engine's equivalent-ball radius; a tall body would plausibly need more mass (hoop conjecture, not verified). Canon questions for the owners: whether work done shoving the surroundings is paid from the absorbed energy or from the endless store (decides whether the loop multiplier 1/(1 − f) applies at all); and whether growth is anchored at the soles (and, if so, whether he is held to the ground). Choices that are ours, to be labelled on the page: the instant time scale (final height ÷ 1,540 m/s); the 1 − cos rate profile; anchoring at the soles; measuring a bystander's distance from his final surface; the top of the head as the fastest shove point; the equivalent-ball side factor. Existing data needing fixes (outside this topic): density_black_hole_rex_2m uses the old 2.54 m³ volume (canon 2.84 m³ gives 2.08e26 kg/m³ and 5.9e26 kg); energy_chicxulub_impact can cite Morgan et al. 2022 (about 5e23 J, abstract 'about 10^23 J'); energy_krakatoa_1883 should note Harkrider & Press's 100–150 Mt air-wave equivalent; blast_kinney_graham_peak_overpressure's ground-reflection question is answered by Baker 1977 (E' = 2E on rigid ground); schwarzschild_radius still cites Wikipedia only.
